zones.name: Flag theory: scattering your life across several countries
zones.essay:
Flag theory is an idea for getting many of the things a private country promises without owning any land. A person places each part of their life under a different country, so that no single government holds all of it. The idea is credited to the investment writer Harry D. Schultz, who proposed three "flags": a second passport, an address in a tax haven, and assets kept outside the home country. It later grew to five, adding a place to run a business and a place to spend money. In the 1980s and 1990s a British company, Scope International, sold books under the name W.G. Hill, possibly a pseudonym, describing the "perpetual traveller". This is someone who keeps moving and never stays long enough to count as a legal resident anywhere, in the hope of owing no income tax, military service or jury duty.

It helps to separate this from founding a territory. Nothing is claimed and no flag is raised. The combination is made of ordinary legal products from real states, which is why no navy has any reason to act against it. The person gets choice among governments and gives up any claim to a place of their own.

Some of the law here is settled. Each country decides who its nationals are. Each country also decides who owes it tax, and the common test is residence, usually looking at days present, a home, family and work. The United States is the large exception. It taxes citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, and the Supreme Court upheld this in Cook v. Tait in 1924 for a citizen living in Mexico. So an American cannot become a perpetual traveller by travelling. The only exit is giving up citizenship, which carries a fee and, for people above set wealth or tax thresholds or behind on their filings, an exit tax treating their assets as sold the day before they leave.

The second settled change is in the banks. Under FATCA, the American law, foreign banks report US account holders to the tax agency. Under the Common Reporting Standard, an international system run through the OECD, banks in about 172 member countries and territories collect each customer's tax home and governments swap the data. A report on the group that oversees this gives 171 million accounts. Suppose a traveller opens an account in a low-tax country and tells the bank "I am tax resident nowhere". The bank has to ask for a tax residence and for proof of it, and an answer it cannot record invites refusal or further questions. The third flag, assets kept abroad out of sight, depended on banks saying nothing, and for most people with ordinary accounts that has ended.

The OECD has also said that certain residence and citizenship by investment schemes may be misused to hide offshore assets, and it monitors what it treats as high-risk schemes. A purchased residence certificate from a low-tax island is therefore something a bank may look at with more suspicion, whatever the paper says.

What remains open is narrower than the old books suggested. Reading the rules as they stand, it seems that no treaty obliges a person to be tax resident somewhere. Each country asks only whether the person is resident there, so a person who truly fails every country's test may owe income tax to none of them. Whether a given person has truly left is decided separately by each country, and home countries can argue that ties remain. That is a question of fact, argued case by case, and there is no international court where a traveller can get one binding answer. The honest position is that being nowhere is possible on paper and hard to prove to the people who ask, such as banks, landlords and immigration officers.

Follow it through a real week. A clinic asks for health cover, and a health insurer wants a country of residence. A child needs a school and a birth record. Staying more than a visitor's allowance needs a visa, and working during the stay needs a permit, so the person lives by the rules of each host in turn. If something goes wrong, the only government with a duty to help is the passport country, and only as far as its own consular practice goes.

The strongest version is modest. A person who is not American holds two real nationalities, keeps one real tax residence in a low-tax country where they spend real time, runs a company somewhere reputable, and reports honestly. That is legal in many cases. A community of such people could gather on a ship or in a rented town, and every member would still sit under the law of the place they are standing and of each country that issued them a document. As a route to sovereignty it gives none. As a way of lowering how much any one state can reach, it does work to a limited degree, as long as the person accepts that every flag can be withdrawn by the state that issued it. Roger Ver, who gave up US citizenship in 2014 after obtaining citizenship of Saint Kitts and Nevis, shows the limit. He was arrested in Spain in April 2024 on a US indictment over tax, and in October 2025 he agreed to pay $49.9 million under a deferred prosecution agreement.

odds.why: Wealthy expatriates already live in versions of this, so the chance of doing it is high. The law score is middling because each country's tax and immigration tests still apply, and bank reporting has removed much of the privacy the idea once offered. Holding on is fairly likely because there is no place to raid, although each state can withdraw what it issued. It creates no state, so recognition is close to nil.

zones.name: Giving up every nationality and living stateless
zones.essay:
Some people who want to live outside every country try to do it with their own legal status instead of with land. They give up their citizenship and hold no other, then say they belong to a new community or to the world. The idea combines the legal act of renouncing a nationality with a replacement identity supplied by a micronation, an online nation or a world citizens' registry. To follow what this does, it helps to know what nationality is for. A nationality is the legal tie that gives a person a government obliged to take them back and entitled to speak up for them abroad. Border systems assume everyone has one.

Two treaties deal with people who have none. The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons defines a stateless person as someone "not considered as a national by any State under the operation of its law". It gives such a person certain rights in countries that have joined it, and Article 28 tells those countries to issue travel documents to stateless people lawfully staying in their territory. Article 32 asks them to make naturalisation easier as far as they can. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness tries to stop the condition arising. Article 7(1)(a) says that where a member state's law allows renunciation, renouncing shall not end a person's nationality unless the person has or acquires another one.

That settles some things plainly. A self-declared nation is not a state, so its citizenship does not stop a person being stateless, and it gives no second nationality in the sense these treaties mean. In a country that has joined the 1961 treaty and applied it, a person trying to renounce into nothing should be refused. The treaties also give no right to enter anywhere. Article 28 applies to people already lawfully staying, and the 1954 treaty says nothing that obliges a state to admit a stateless stranger.

Not every country has joined, and the United States has long allowed a person to renounce without holding another nationality, while warning that the person will lack any government's protection and may have difficulty travelling. So the door is open in some places. Garry Davis walked through it on 25 May 1948 at the American embassy in Paris, saying he was a citizen of the world. He founded a registry in 1949 and the World Government of World Citizens in 1953, and he travelled on his own World Passport for 65 years, regularly arrested and expelled. He had a public profile and supporters. His customers had less.

Suppose a person does this today. On the day after renunciation the person is a foreigner in whatever country they stand in, with no passport and no right to stay. The host may tolerate them, grant a stay and travel document if it follows the 1954 treaty, or try to remove them. Removal is hard, since no country must take the person, and this is how people end up held in detention or stuck in transit. Mehran Karimi Nasseri lived in a French airport terminal from 1988 to 2006 without accepted papers. Everyday life then gets narrower. Banks must identify customers and record a tax residence and a nationality. Employers must check a right to work. Airlines refuse boarding to someone a destination will not admit, since they carry the cost of returning them. Marriage, inheritance and registering a child all ask for documents. Article 1 of the 1961 treaty helps the next generation in one way, requiring a member state to give nationality to a person born in its territory who would otherwise be stateless, so a child may not inherit the condition, depending on where the birth happens.

Tax does not disappear either. Most countries tax by residence, so a stateless person living somewhere pays there. The former country may pursue earlier debts. The US exit tax applies to the wealthy and to those behind on filings regardless of what happens next.

What is open is whether a person may refuse all nationalities as a matter of right. Article 7(1)(b) of the 1961 treaty contains an exception, saying the bar on renouncing does not apply where it would be inconsistent with the principles of Articles 13 and 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which concern movement and asylum. That wording seems aimed at people fleeing persecution. Reading the text, it does not seem to create a general right to be stateless by choice. No court ruling on that exact question is known. It is also an open point how far a host must help someone who made themselves stateless on purpose, since the 1954 definition asks only whether any state counts the person as a national and says nothing about how it happened. On its face that covers a voluntary case, and states may read it more narrowly in practice.

The potential is small and personal. The strongest version is a person with a tolerant host that has joined the 1954 treaty, who renounces in a country that allows it, obtains a stateless person's travel document, and lives on it. That person then depends on one host's goodwill, which is more dependent than before. For a community the idea gives nothing to build on. Each member would lose the consular help, travel rights and proof of identity that other routes rely on.

odds.why: A person can renounce in some countries, and treaty members should refuse it, so reaching this status is possible but not universal. Once stateless, the person has no right to enter anywhere and cannot easily bank or work. Holding on is low because a host can detain or restrict such a person with little outside objection. It creates no state, so nothing exists to recognise.

zones.name: Bought citizenship stacked with a private community
zones.essay:
Citizenship by investment is a programme in which a country grants its nationality in return for a payment or investment. A private community is a town, estate or zone run by a company or association under contract with its residents. Stacking the two means that a group of like-minded people each buy the same small country's passport, or arrange a deal with that country, and then live together on private land there. The appeal is that they would hold a real nationality, with a real seat at the United Nations behind it, and live by their own contract rules, with the state at a distance because it was paid to stay friendly. No new state is founded, and the group lives under one that already exists.

The first thing that is settled is that a country may grant its nationality on its own terms, as a matter of its own law. A passport bought this way is a real passport. The second settled point comes from the International Court of Justice in Nottebohm, a 1955 case. Friedrich Nottebohm, a German who had lived in Guatemala since 1905, obtained Liechtenstein nationality during a short visit to Europe in 1939. Liechtenstein later sued Guatemala on his behalf, and the Court held the claim inadmissible. Nationality granted without a genuine connection did not entitle Liechtenstein to protect him against Guatemala, the country where he actually lived. The Court did not say the nationality was void inside Liechtenstein. So a bought passport works for travel where states accept it, and it may not give the person a government able to press a claim against their long-time country of residence.

The third settled point is new and applies within Europe. On 29 April 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in Commission v Malta, case C-181/23, that Malta had broken EU law by running a scheme that gave nationality through a transactional procedure in exchange for set payments. The Court called this the commercialisation of nationality and, through it, of EU citizenship. It relied on EU treaties and on the relationship of solidarity and good faith between a state and its nationals. Malta had argued that a prior genuine link was not required by international law and that Nottebohm did not supply it, and the Court's ruling was grounded in EU law. So the ruling closes the route for EU member states. It does not bind Caribbean or Pacific programmes.

Those programmes depend on outsiders in another way. Much of a passport's value is its visa-free access. The European Commission proposed suspending the visa waiver for Vanuatu over its scheme, which charged about $130,000. The Commission pointed to a very low rejection rate and to citizenship granted to people listed in Interpol's databases, and the EU Council then partially suspended the waiver. The partner state can hold firm and its passport can still lose value overnight. The OECD monitors high-risk schemes because they can be used to get around bank reporting. A bank may therefore ask a holder for proof of real ties.

The Comoros shows a third way this can fail. Around a decade before 2018 the Comoros Islands agreed with the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait to sell citizenship to stateless people in those countries, known as Bidoon, in return for development money. In 2018 its parliament reported that nearly 48,000 foreigners had received passports, that thousands were sold outside official channels by what it called mafia networks, and that up to $100 million had gone missing. When a small state sells nationality in bulk, the buyers depend on that state's own honesty and politics.

Now suppose the community stage. A group of 2,000 people buys the passports of an island country and buys private land there. They write a contract covering rules of the estate, private arbitration and shared services. On the estate, ordinary property and contract law gives them a good deal of freedom, as in a large condominium or gated town. But criminal law, immigration, tax, building rules and the courts all remain the state's. Being citizens gives them something foreigners lack, which is the right to stay and a right to vote, so a group of that size in a very small country could become politically important. Reading the rules of ordinary democracy, it seems such a group could lawfully try to elect representatives and seek a special law. The Free State Project and the takeover of Antelope, Oregon, by followers of Rajneesh show how moving voters can work and how it can provoke a response. Whether local voters would tolerate a bought-in bloc is a political question nobody can answer in advance.

The state's position is the open part. Nothing in international law stops a small state from giving such a community a special zone, and a later government can reverse it. Honduras's Supreme Court struck down its zone laws in 2024 with retroactive effect. Whether a state that sells its nationality to a group has any wider duty to the group is untested. Nobody has tested the full stack of mass citizenship plus a governing contract in one place.

The potential is real but limited to the level of a very favourable host deal. The strongest version is a stable small state that passes a special zone law after a real public debate, a community whose members actually move there and live there, so that Nottebohm's genuine connection grows over time, and an investment treaty behind the zone. The support of the country's own voters would decide how long it lasts. The group would get strong autonomy under a real flag, and a later law could end it.

odds.why: Citizenship programmes exist and private estates exist, so joining them is feasible, but no group has yet bought a shared nationality and a governing charter together. The law score reflects that each piece is lawful under the host's law and that the EU route has been closed by the Malta ruling. Money works through the host's banks, with extra scrutiny. A later government can reverse the deal, as Honduras did, which keeps holding below even odds.

rules.says: A state cannot press a claim for a national against another state unless the nationality reflects a genuine connection.

zones.name: E-residency plus a company as a community's legal shell
zones.essay:
A digital community has a problem when it wants to own anything. It has members and ideas, and no legal person that can sign a lease, hold a bank account or be sued. One answer combines two things that real states already sell to foreigners. The first is e-residency, a digital identity a state gives to non-citizens so that they can sign documents and run a company online. The second is a company, or a foundation, registered in that state, which acts as the legal body of the community. Members become its owners or members, and its charter becomes the community's constitution in practice.

Estonia is the leading example. It launched e-Residency at the end of 2014, and its official figures show over 144,000 e-residents from 187 countries and more than 44,000 companies. The state took in nearly €125 million from the programme in 2025. It does this for revenue and talent, and that is why the offer is reliable, since Estonia gains from keeping it open.

Some things here are settled. An e-resident is not a citizen, gets no right to live in Estonia, and holds no passport. A company formed this way is an ordinary Estonian company under Estonian company and tax law. The founder remains under the law of wherever they live. Suppose 500 people in thirty countries form a company as their community's shell. Estonian law governs the company. Each member's home country still taxes them on what they earn, and each home country's rules on foreign holdings apply to their share. If the group sells memberships with a promise of profit, securities law in every country where buyers live can apply. In 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued over bonds offered for New Utopia, a nation that was never built, and that case began with a website.

The less obvious settled part is reporting. Banks must find out who really owns and controls a company, and under the Common Reporting Standard they report accounts to the tax authorities of the owner's home. A company with hundreds of foreign members has more to explain, and a bank's compliance office may simply decline. A shell in a reputable country gets a hearing, which is more than a micronation's charter gets, and it does not guarantee an account.

Tax on the company itself is less tidy. As a general rule of tax law, many countries treat a company as resident where it is really managed, or as having a taxable presence where its people work. Reading those rules, it seems that a company run day to day by a founder in Berlin may be taxed in Germany as well as Estonia, whatever its papers say. Each country applies its own test, and the answer can differ. That is an uncertainty about facts more than about law, and many small online firms live with it.

What is open is how far this shell can stretch toward government. Nothing in Estonian company law appears designed to stop a company from calling its shareholders citizens in its own documents. Reading the law of contract, members can agree to a code of conduct, to pay dues and to take disputes to a private arbitrator. Whether a court would enforce a sanction such as expulsion with loss of assets depends on the host's company law and consumer law, and no court is known to have considered a community built this way. Whether a state would tolerate its company brand being used for a project claiming sovereignty is also untested. A state might view that as harmless or as a reputational problem, and it has ordinary powers to strike off a company or remove an e-resident's status. The Network School in Malaysia is the nearest warning, though it concerned a physical site. In July 2026 a city council revoked its business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions, after a political row about its aims, and ordered it to stop the next day.

There are real limits on what the shell can ever do. It cannot issue a nationality, so every member needs a real passport. It cannot arrest anyone or keep anyone in, and locking up a member would expose the organisers to criminal law. It cannot make treaties, because the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties covers agreements between states, and it can only sign contracts. It cannot issue money with legal force. Its radio, ships and aircraft, if it had any, would need state licences of the ordinary kind.

The potential is that of a strong club with a real legal skeleton. The strongest version is a foundation or company in a stable state with a published charter, an honest statement that membership is no nationality, independent audits, and members who pay their taxes at home. Such a body can buy land, employ staff, hold a treasury, run schools, insure members as a group where insurers agree, and last for decades, much as some churches and professional bodies do. It could also move, since a company can often be re-formed in another country. Its home state could still end the arrangement, and the members would keep their ordinary lives. Building such a body is well within reach. Becoming a state by this path has no known precedent, and no government would have to acknowledge such a claim.

odds.why: E-residency is open to applicants and companies can be formed online, so this exists today in ordinary form. The law score is high because it is lawful inside a real state's system, and low only on any claim of government. Bank accounts are possible and not guaranteed for a company with many foreign members. Its host can strike it off, though it would have little reason to if the body stays out of trouble.

rules.says: A digital identity for foreigners. It gives no citizenship, no residence right and no passport.

zones.name: A DAO legal entity as a government-like shell
zones.essay:
A DAO, or decentralised autonomous organisation, is a group that takes decisions and holds money through software running on a blockchain, a shared public ledger that no single person controls. Members usually vote using tokens, and the software carries out some decisions on its own. To people who want a country without land, this looks like a government already, with a written set of rules, votes, a treasury and members around the world. The combination here is that software plus a law from a real state that gives the group a legal body.

Without such a law the position is uncomfortable. In November 2024 a US federal court in California, in Samuels v. Lido DAO, found that a buyer had adequately pleaded that Lido DAO was a general partnership. In a partnership each partner can be personally liable for the whole group's debts. The court rejected the argument that the DAO was only software, saying its acts were "the actions of an entity run by people". The ruling came at an early stage of the case, and the claimant named only three large investors said to play important governance roles. It is still unclear which ordinary token holders could count as partners. Other US cases have pointed the same way, including a California ruling that a DAO's members could be treated as general partners and a federal regulator's enforcement action against Ooki DAO. So the law has not decided the outer edge, and it has made clear that calling a group software gives no shelter.

Several legislatures have offered a legal form in response. Wyoming was the first US state, in 2021, letting a DAO register as a kind of limited liability company, with a 2022 amendment allowing management by members or by algorithm. Tennessee and Vermont have also passed laws allowing DAOs to form as limited liability companies. Wyoming later added a further form. Utah's act, signed on 13 March 2023 and effective on 1 January 2024, created a distinct entity called the limited liability DAO. Members are liable only for their on-chain contributions, except that those who vote to disobey a court order can be personally liable. It must be formed by at least one natural person and show the state that its code has undergone quality assurance. The Marshall Islands, an independent country, passed a law in 2022 and a second in 2023. According to a legal commentary, the 2022 law required only one person to give identity details to the registry, and the 2023 law added series, where sub-DAOs hold separate assets and liabilities.

These laws settle something modest. A registered DAO can own property, sign contracts and limit members' liability under that jurisdiction's law. CityDAO used Wyoming's law to buy 40 acres near Cody in 2021. Its 6,500 or so "citizens" hold a token, and county zoning still applied to the land. Each law also keeps a human link, in the form of a registered person, an identifier in the filing or a named founder. A state regulator and a court therefore have someone to find. No law listed here gives a DAO any authority over land or people beyond what a company has.

The Marshall Islands law raises the most interesting grey point. It comes from a recognised state, so the entity is a real legal person. Series DAOs resemble a federation of provinces on paper. Reading the idea through ordinary company law, it seems that a foreign court would usually accept that an entity exists, and might still ask whether the protection of its members should hold when the people and the harm are in that court's country. Nobody has fully tested whether a US or European court would respect the limited liability of a nearly anonymous Marshall Islands DAO against a local injured party. The Lido ruling suggests some judges will look at what the people actually do. That question remains open.

Follow the shell through a practical case. Suppose a DAO with a treasury in tokens wants to pay a builder in Portugal. The builder wants euros. A regulated exchange converts the tokens, and it must identify the sender under the Financial Action Task Force's Travel Rule and must check sanctions lists. If token sales promised returns, securities regulators can ask questions, and in the EU a token offered to the public needs a white paper under MiCA, the EU's crypto rules. If a sanctioned person votes or holds tokens, American members may have exposure. Developers can be reached as well. In 2023 two developers of the mixing software Tornado Cash were charged in the United States, and one was convicted on one count in 2025, even after an appeals court said the software itself could not be sanctioned.

The potential is real for governance and small for sovereignty. The strongest version is a DAO registered in a recognised state, with a real legal officer, honest disclosure to token buyers, ordinary tax compliance, and members who vote on a shared treasury and shared land. This could run schools, hold conservation land or manage services for thousands of people, and its records would be hard to falsify on the chain. Assets it holds on the blockchain are also harder for a court to freeze than a bank account, though the people holding the keys remain within reach. It would still be a company under some state's law, which can amend the statute at any time. Calling its members citizens changes nothing in the eyes of any other government.

odds.why: Registering a DAO costs little and several places allow it, so forming one is easy. The law score is middling because the entity is valid, while courts have shown they will look through unregistered DAOs and nothing in these statutes grants government powers. Money is limited at the point where tokens meet banks and regulated exchanges. A server-free ledger is hard to close, but the people running it can be sued or charged.

zones.name: Private courts enforced through the New York Convention
zones.essay:
A court needs a government behind it. Arbitration is the way around that for some disputes. Two parties agree in a contract that a private person will decide any quarrel between them. Governments have agreed to enforce the result as if a court had given it, and this is the closest thing the world has to a private legal system with state force behind it. People designing new communities therefore ask whether residents could live under a contract with a private court, enforced through the world's courts, with no government of their own. This combines a governing contract, a private court and a treaty.

The treaty is the 1958 New York Convention on foreign arbitral awards. The law it sets is clear. Under Article II, each member state must recognise a written agreement to arbitrate and send the parties to arbitration if one of them goes to court instead. Under Article III, each must enforce awards as binding. Article V gives short grounds for refusing. These include a party's incapacity, an invalid agreement, a party not given proper notice or a chance to present its case, and a tribunal that went beyond what was agreed. A court may also refuse where the subject cannot be settled by arbitration under its own law, or where enforcing would be contrary to its public policy. Those last two grounds set the outer limit. A murder cannot be arbitrated, and reading those grounds, neither can anything a state insists on deciding itself. So private law by contract can reach commerce, property use, service fees and many civil disputes, and it stops short of crime and of matters each country reserves.

The agreement is what gives it force, and that sets a second limit. Arbitration binds people who agreed. The Sulu heirs' claim shows what happens without clear consent. An arbitrator in Spain and then Paris awarded $14.92 billion against Malaysia on an 1878 paper, and French courts dismantled it, holding that no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia. A neighbour, a visitor or a child born in the community has signed nothing. A community contract could bind adult members and leave outsiders untouched.

Article I raises the point most relevant to places outside every country. The treaty covers awards "made in the territory of a State" other than the one where enforcement is sought. An arbitration normally has a legal home, called its seat. A commentator on blockchain justice notes that awards with no seat risk falling outside the treaty. Reading the text, it seems that an award stated to be made on a platform on the high seas, or in a self-declared state, would not be made in the territory of any member state, so a court need not treat it as a Convention award. Parties can avoid this by naming a seat in a real state, even when no one travels there. Whether a ship under a flag counts as the flag state's territory for this purpose is not answered by the text, and no ruling on it is known. The modern practice of a legal seat suggests that lawyers would simply name a land seat, which puts the project back under that state's courts. Those courts can set an award aside.

Belgium once tried removing that supervision. A 1985 law ended the setting aside of awards made in Belgium when no party had a link there. According to the arbitration lawyer Bernard Hanotiau, it deterred more parties than it attracted, and the law was repealed in 1998.

Three real designs show the range. Kleros is a blockchain protocol in which token holders serve as randomly chosen jurors. In Mexico in 2021 a court enforced an award in a lease dispute. A human arbitrator had absorbed a Kleros result into a conventional award, so the court enforced the human's award and not the protocol's ruling. Whether a pure on-chain decision by pseudonymous jurors can satisfy Article V's requirement of a fair hearing is debated and untested. Supporters point to self-enforcing transfers on the chain, which need no court when the assets are on the chain.

The Dubai International Financial Centre shows how a state's support cuts both ways. Its DIFC-LCIA centre, whose name joined the zone with the London Court of International Arbitration, was abolished by Dubai Decree 34 of 2021, effective 20 September, with its rights and duties passed to the Dubai International Arbitration Centre. Parties' old agreements were deemed valid. In Narciso v Nash in 2024 the DIFC court upheld one such clause. The zone's law survived, and a single decree still ended an institution.

Próspera goes furthest. Honduras's zone law required binding arbitration for contract and property matters. Residents sign an Agreement of Coexistence. The default provider, the Próspera Arbitration Center, is a Texas company with a public, court-like track producing binding precedents and rules for eviction, labour and small claims. Honduras is a party to the New York Convention. Practitioners writing about it warn that arbitration without a clear agreement could raise questions of consent before a foreign enforcing court. Honduras's Supreme Court held the zone laws unconstitutional in September 2024. What this means for those awards has not been tested.

Scholars disagree about the historical model. Milgrom, North and Weingast wrote in 1990 that medieval merchants at the Champagne Fairs evolved a private code without state enforcement. Emily Kadens argued in 2012 that the customary law merchant is largely a myth, since widespread commercial law came from contract and statute. Stephen Sachs showed that English fair courts were neither set up by merchants nor staffed by merchant judges. The history therefore gives weak support to a law with no state.

The strongest version is a community with signed adult contracts, a named seat in a respected country, a fair procedure and limits to civil matters. That is achievable. It is a private legal order inside state law, and a state court keeps the final word.

odds.why: Arbitration clauses are in everyday use, so a community using one is easy to set up. The New York Convention gives such awards real force, up to the limits in Article V on public policy and matters that cannot be arbitrated. Criminal matters and people who never signed stay out of reach. It creates no state, though a private court cannot be closed by a raid in the way a platform can.

Courts must recognise written arbitration agreements on matters capable of settlement by arbitration.
Enforcement may be refused for invalid agreements, unfair procedure, non-arbitrable subjects or public policy.

zones.name: Private currency with an offshore bank or crypto treasury
zones.essay:
A country usually has its own money and a central bank. A private project can try to copy this by combining a private currency, printed or digital, with a treasury kept somewhere outside its home government's easy reach. That treasury might be an account at an offshore bank, a bank the project charters for itself, or crypto held in wallets the project controls. The hope is that members can trade among themselves, that the project can pay for things, and that no government can freeze the money. Each piece has a history, and most of the history is of prosecutions.

Some of this is settled. Inside a country, that country's criminal law applies to anyone who issues money-like things there. Bernard von NotHaus minted Liberty Dollars in the United States, coins worth about $7 million in total according to the FBI. On 18 March 2011 a federal jury in North Carolina convicted him of making coins resembling US coins, of issuing and passing them as current money, and of conspiracy. The government's release said it is a federal violation to create private coin or currency systems to compete with the official coinage. Its prosecutor called such attempts a form of domestic terrorism. That case turned on metal coins resembling US money, so its reach over a clearly different token is less certain.

Digital private money met the same fate through a different law. Liberty Reserve, based in Costa Rica, let users move money with only a name, an email address and a birth date, and made no effort to verify identities. Costa Rica told it in 2009 that it needed a licence, and refused one in 2011. In May 2013 US prosecutors shut it down under the Patriot Act after an investigation across 17 countries, alleging more than $6 billion in laundering, and charged its founder Arthur Budovsky and six others. Moving offshore did not put it out of reach, because its customers and its dollars passed through places the United States could reach.

An offshore bank does not solve this. A bank in the ordinary sense needs a licence from a supervisor other banks trust, a correspondent bank to reach the world, and access to SWIFT, the messaging network banks use. A self-chartered bank has none of these. The Dominion of Melchizedek claimed to have sold about 300 bank licences, and that history is one reason compliance officers treat such licences with suspicion. A licensed bank in a low-tax country is available, and it reports account holders under the Common Reporting Standard and FATCA.

Currency codes are a smaller, real obstacle. Banks book payments using the ISO 4217 list of three-letter codes, and a new currency has no listed code. Even unrecognised governments with real economies run into exchange problems. The Somaliland shilling cannot easily be exchanged outside Somaliland, and the Transnistrian ruble can be exchanged only inside the territory. A state does not guarantee its way out of this either. The Marshall Islands passed a Sovereign Currency Act in 2018 for a national digital currency called SOV, and the International Monetary Fund opposed it. The plan later wound down. That was a recognised state, and it still could not make the idea work.

Crypto is where the law is most unsettled. Holding a token in a wallet needs no bank. Nothing about the software requires anyone's permission, and a court order has to be aimed at a person. In August 2022 the US Treasury sanctioned the mixing software Tornado Cash. On 26 November 2024 the Fifth Circuit appeals court in Van Loon held that its immutable smart contracts do not qualify as "property" under federal law, so the sanctions office lacked authority to sanction the software as such. In March 2025 the Treasury lifted those sanctions. The people were treated differently. A Dutch court sentenced developer Alexey Pertsev to 5 years and 4 months in 2024, and in 2025 a US jury found Roman Storm guilty of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, on one of three charges. So what remains open is how far software that no one controls is beyond sanctions in other courts and under other laws, and how far writing such software makes a person a money transmitter. One appeals court's reading of one statute does not answer those questions worldwide.

Follow a treasury through a real month. Suppose a community holds $20 million in stablecoins, tokens tied to the dollar, and wants to buy diesel. The fuel supplier wants dollars in a bank. A regulated exchange must identify the sender and the recipient under the Travel Rule, the international standard on money transfers, and must check sanctions lists. Stablecoin issuers can often freeze tokens at a regulator's request, and in the United States issuers now fall under the GENIUS Act of 2025. If tokens were sold to members with hope of profit, the regulators who sued over New Utopia's bonds can come back in, and EU buyers bring in the MiCA rules. Any American running the accounts is bound by US sanctions wherever they sit. Reading the money transmission cases, it seems that if the community's treasury moves funds on behalf of members, the person doing it could be treated as an unlicensed transmitter in the places members live, though the result would vary by country and has not been tested for a self-described national treasury.

The potential is modest and real. The raam, issued by the Global Country of World Peace, was accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands. A closed token that works as membership credit or a local exchange unit is a common idea, kept small and not represented as legal money. The strongest version has a token used only among members for goods and services, no promise of profit, and a reserve of ordinary money in a licensed bank or regulated custodian, with honest tax reporting by members. This gives a community an internal economy. Outside its circle, every payment still crosses into a system run by states, and the community would be a customer of that system.

odds.why: Issuing a token or a coin is cheap, so starting is easy. The record of Liberty Dollar and Liberty Reserve shows prosecution when private money reaches the public at scale, which keeps the law and holding scores low. The money score is low because food, fuel and medicine are bought in official currency through regulated firms. The Tornado Cash ruling shows open questions on code, while the people behind it were still prosecuted.

zones.name: Special status at international bodies in place of statehood
zones.essay:
Most people assume a body is either a country at the United Nations or nothing. There is a middle ground. Some bodies that are not ordinary states have won a seat near the table, with standing in diplomatic rooms and immunity from some national laws. A project with no land could try to combine real international work with such a status, and so gain much of what recognition gives without being a state. To see whether it could, it helps to look at who has it and how.

The UN's own list is short. Two non-members hold a standing invitation as observers and keep permanent missions, the Holy See and the State of Palestine. The General Assembly gave Palestine non-member observer state status by resolution 67/19 on 29 November 2012. Other entities with a standing invitation include the International Committee of the Red Cross, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Olympic Committee, the Inter-Parliamentary Union and the Sovereign Order of Malta. These lists are decided by the General Assembly, so member states control entry. That much is settled. A body cannot apply itself into observer status against the wishes of the majority, and observer status is not membership or a vote in the Assembly. Whether such a resolution makes something a state is a separate matter. No general rule says that it does, and governments continue to differ on Palestine.

Each of those bodies got there through its own history. The Holy See has the Catholic Church behind it and Vatican City under the 1929 Lateran Treaty with Italy. The Order of Malta ruled Rhodes and Malta for centuries, lost its last land in 1798, and kept diplomatic ties with more than 100 states because they chose to continue them. It became a UN observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. The Order issues passports, coins and stamps and signs treaties, and it counts only three senior officers as citizens.

The Red Cross is a different and more useful case. The International Committee of the Red Cross is a private Swiss association and it is not sovereign. Its status comes from a job states gave it. The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 name it in their text, so it is written into treaties. On 19 March 1993 it signed a formal agreement with Switzerland that protects its property and archives, gives staff legal immunity, exempts it from taxes and gives it secure communications at the level of embassies. Switzerland does not recognise passports issued by it. It has similar agreements with other governments. A private body has therefore gained many of the practical protections of a state, by being useful to all sides in war.

The International Olympic Committee shows a further use of status, which is giving standing to others. Taiwan's team competes as Chinese Taipei under a formula worked out after the IOC recognised the People's Republic's committee in 1979. Taiwan uses the same name at APEC, the Pacific trade forum, and takes part in the World Trade Organization as a Separate Customs Territory. Those memberships exist because the bodies' rules allow non-state economies or sports teams to take part. That gives a template for a place with no recognition, and Taiwan's size and trade are what bring the others to the table.

For a new community, the first thing to separate is ordinary accreditation from special status. Non-governmental organisations can seek accreditation at the UN's Economic and Social Council, which is a route to attend meetings and gives no diplomatic standing. The Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, founded in 1991, works as an advocacy body for peoples without seats. Suppose a new group spends twenty years running a hospital ship or disaster relief. Governments may sign agreements letting it work in their waters, with duty-free passage and some protection for staff. Reading the Red Cross and Order of Malta examples, it seems that immunity agreements can be won one state at a time, on the strength of a service states want, and that a host government must agree first. No self-declared nation is known to have gained anything like this from scratch.

The open questions are these. It is not settled whether a body with a standing invitation has any right to keep it, since the Assembly could in principle change its mind. It is also not settled how far the Order of Malta's standing rests on sovereignty at all, as against a long habit among states. Nobody can say in advance how many agreements would be enough for others to treat a new body as an international person, because the question has no threshold in any treaty.

Money and paper follow the status. A body with a host agreement can usually bank and move goods with less friction. Its staff keep their own nationalities and tax homes. Its immunity covers what the agreement says and no more, and residents of a community would not be covered unless they are staff on official business. Passports issued by such a body work only with states that have agreed, as the Order's do.

The potential is low for a new body and real over long periods. The strongest version is a neutral service organisation that does something states need and cannot easily do themselves, wins a headquarters agreement, then gains named roles in treaties. It would have to give up any claim to rule people or land, because the immunity is granted for the work. Such a body might last a very long time and would remain something other than a state. A founder seeking a place to live under their own laws would not get that from this route.

odds.why: A new group winning a standing UN invitation in 25 years is very unlikely, since the existing holders rest on centuries of history, a church, a treaty role or a national claim. Lesser host agreements are more realistic, and they take decades of useful work. Once granted, status tends to last, which explains the higher holding figure. Status like this is itself a substitute for recognition and rarely leads to it.

zones.name: Having friendly states create a treaty body for a community
zones.essay:
An international organisation is a body set up by a treaty among states, such as a UN agency. It is treated in international law as a legal person, separate from its members, and it usually gets immunities from the host country in a headquarters agreement. The idea here is a shortcut. A private community or foundation persuades a few friendly small states to sign a treaty creating an organisation around it. The result would be neither a state nor a company. It would be an international body with immunity for its premises and staff, a legal standing that private bodies lack, and a place in diplomatic life. This combines a private project, a host deal and a small treaty.

This has actually happened in a limited way, and the example shows both what works and what it takes. The Global Green Growth Institute began as a think tank in 2010, started by the then President of South Korea, Lee Myung-bak. In 2012 it was turned into a treaty-based international organisation, a change formalised at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil. It has an Assembly of member countries and a Council. Membership is open to any UN member state that shares its aims. So a body that started as a non-state institute did convert into an international organisation, and it took a sitting head of government and a group of states willing to sign.

What is settled is that treaties are made by states. Article 6 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties says every state can make them, and Article 3 notes that international agreements can also exist with other subjects of international law. A private group cannot give itself this status by signing with itself. Any treaty needs at least two real governments, and each one's constitution decides who may sign and whether parliament must approve. Nothing in general international law limits how small those states may be. Small states already earn money from legal services. Tonga rents satellite slots, Nauru sponsored a mining company at the International Seabed Authority, and the Marshall Islands runs a registry.

What such a body gets is defined by its treaty and its host agreement. The Red Cross's agreement with Switzerland shows the kind of thing a host might offer, with immunity for staff, protected premises, tax exemption and secure communications. A UN headquarters district shows the limit, since most local law still applies inside. Host agreements usually cover official acts, so a resident who commits a theft or owes tax would remain under ordinary law.

Follow the steps. Suppose a foundation persuades two small states to sign a treaty, with one hosting. The first challenge is the parties' own politics, since opposition parties can attack a deal that looks like selling sovereignty. Honduras's reversal of its zones, and the $10.8 billion claim that followed, would be on every minister's mind. Next is outside recognition. Other states are not bound by a treaty they did not sign, so a third country need not grant immunity, accept the body's documents or treat its staff as officials. Banks ask who regulates it, and an international organisation with no known member states will look to them like the Melchizedek licences of the 1990s. The International Civil Aviation Organization's passport standard does list codes for certain organisations, such as the UN, but a new body would have to be added, and no state must honour its papers. Sanctions and money laundering rules apply through the banks, and a founder's own nationality can keep them under home law for crimes abroad.

The open questions are real. No treaty sets a minimum number of members for an organisation to count as a true international person. It is not settled whether third states owe any respect to a body created by only two tiny states to house a private community. No court has ruled on such a design, since none has been built. Whether a state may in effect hand its treaty power to a private sponsor by signing whatever it brings is also unsettled. Reading the Vienna Convention, it seems that a treaty is valid so long as states freely consent, and it does not ask why they want it. A later government could still withdraw under the treaty's terms, and if the host withdraws, the body has nowhere to stand.

Fake versions are a known hazard. The Dominion of Melchizedek sold passports and bank licences on the strength of claims to standing, and the Marshall Islands publicly condemned those claims in 1998. A real treaty is ratified by named governments, and that can be checked.

There is potential here, and it is probably the most legally solid way for a paper project to gain standing, short of a state's own act. The strongest version is an honest public-interest mission such as ocean rescue, climate records or stateless people's documents, with several states of different regions as members, a public treaty and a real budget. It might gain immunity for its site, an observer seat at some forums and the right to sign agreements. It would have a purpose defined by treaty and be answerable to its member states, so a community that wanted to live by its own rules would have exchanged a government above it for a council of governments above it.

odds.why: One think tank has converted into a treaty body, with a president's backing, and a private community doing so is much harder. If real states ratify a treaty, the legal position is strong, which is why the law score is high. Banking depends on who the member states are. Host withdrawal is the main risk, and non-member states are never bound. It would be an international organisation, so recognition as a state is not what it would get.

zones.name: An online community buying scattered plots of land
zones.essay:
The network state is an idea set out by Balaji Srinivasan in a 2022 book. A community forms online around shared values, pools its money, buys land in many places, and later seeks diplomatic recognition from real governments. It reverses the usual order, in which land comes first. On a map, the result would look like an archipelago, with houses and buildings scattered among other countries and joined by the internet. This combines an online nation, private land purchase and a later claim to statehood.

The most important settled point is the difference between owning land and ruling it. A deed gives a person rights under the law of the country where the land lies. It gives no authority to make law there. Kiribati, a full UN member, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for the Natoavatu estate in Fiji, and the land stayed under Fiji's law. If a sovereign state buying land gets no sovereignty with the deed, a private group gets none. Each plot therefore has its own government. A plot in Wyoming follows county zoning and state law, as CityDAO found when it bought 40 acres near Cody and learned that zoning may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot. A plot in Portugal follows Portuguese law, tax and building rules. Many countries also limit land purchases by foreigners or foreign companies, so a single community may have to buy through a different local company in each country.

Follow one plot. The community's foundation buys a farm through a local company and builds cabins. A local council asks whether the use is residential or commercial. If members come from abroad, each needs a visa and a right to stay. If they work there, a permit. Rent and profit are taxed locally. If someone is hurt, a local court hears the case. If a neighbour complains, or if politics turn, the licence can go. The Network School shows how fast. It ran from a hotel in Forest City in Malaysia as an ordinary business with a council licence. After a row in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the licence on 21 July and ordered it to stop the next day. Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum to host a campus, which opened in Astana on 2 September. The two facts belong together. A host can end a site quickly, and a mobile community can find another host.

Scattered holdings do give something. Risk is spread, since one country's decision touches only one plot. Money and members can flow to whichever site is working. A site also gives a physical place to meet, which an online nation lacks. Praxis has spent years looking for such a site, and each candidate has needed a host government's agreement.

The history people cite most often as a precedent is contested and differs in important ways. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, raised money from a worldwide diaspora to buy land in Ottoman and then British-ruled Palestine, and it was incorporated in London in 1907. By 1948 it held about 54 percent of the land in Jewish hands, a bit under 4 percent of Mandatory Palestine. Statehood in 1948 came through UN debate, war and displacement that the land purchases did not decide, and the legitimacy of later land transfers has been questioned. So the case shows that a diaspora can buy land for a national goal for decades, and it does not show that purchases produce a state.

What is genuinely open is recognition of a state with no contiguous land. The Montevideo Convention's test asks for a "defined territory", and it says nothing about the land being in one piece. Reading the text, it seems that scattered territory could in principle count, as states with enclaves and islands show. That helps only if those pieces have been given up by their current sovereign, and private title does not do that. The theory's answer is that a large enough community would have the numbers and money to bargain for recognition or for special zones. Srinivasan and his supporters argue this. Critics in Malaysia and elsewhere object to the sovereignty aims themselves. No such recognition has ever been granted, so no one can say what number of members or what level of money would matter. Article 3 of the Convention says statehood does not depend on recognition, yet it does not remove the territory test.

There is a further indirect limit. A community with thousands of members and a treasury is a target for securities law if it sold tokens with hope of profit, and for tax authorities and banks, which look at who controls the money. Founders stay under the law of their own nationality. Praxis's reported $500 million facility depended on listing tokens on a public exchange, which puts it in regulated hands.

The potential is the highest in the digital family, as a network of real places, and it is low as a state. The strongest version is a foundation that buys only where the law allows, follows every zoning and visa rule, negotiates with willing governments for campus status, and treats recognition as a distant goal. It could produce real towns with a shared culture and a shared legal contract among members. In 25 years it may hold a good deal of land, each plot under a different flag, with a real chance at a special economic zone somewhere. The members would remain citizens of their own countries unless a state chose to do otherwise.

odds.why: Buying land through companies is ordinary, and groups have done it, though nothing yet joins many sites at scale. The law score reflects that each plot stays under local law, with no legal route from title to authority. Holding is near even, since one site can close while others last, as the Network School's move from Malaysia to Kazakhstan shows. No such project has been recognised, and the theory is untested.

zones.name: Treaties among unrecognised entities
zones.essay:
A country proves it is a country partly by signing treaties. Places that nobody recognises sometimes try a substitute. They sign treaties with each other, exchange ambassadors and form unions, so that a small circle treats each member as a state. There are three levels to this, and they differ a great deal. Real governments of breakaway regions do it. Advocacy groups of stateless peoples do it. Micronations, which are often hobby or art projects, do it too. The question is whether any of this creates legal standing, or whether it is a useful fiction.

Begin with what the law says. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the treaty on how treaties work, covers agreements between states, and Article 6 says every state has capacity to make them. Article 3 says the Convention's limits do not take away the legal force of agreements between states and other subjects of international law, or between such other subjects. So international law does accept that some non-state bodies can make agreements. It does not say who those subjects are. Article 34 adds that a treaty creates no obligations or rights for a third state without its consent. It follows that nothing signed in such a circle binds any outside government. That is settled.

The open part is whether a real breakaway government has treaty capacity at all. There are two old schools of thought. One holds that a place becomes a state by meeting the tests of statehood, whatever others think, and Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention leans this way. The other holds that recognition by others is what makes a state in practice. On the first view, a place with real population, land and government, such as Abkhazia or Somaliland, might sign a real treaty with its peer. On the second view it signs a private paper. No international court has ruled on the status of such a treaty in a way that settles this. What is not in doubt is that a micronation with no territory or population fails the Montevideo test on either view, so its treaty is a contract at most, and often only a statement.

The best-known union is the Community for Democracy and Rights of Nations, called the Commonwealth of Unrecognized States or CIS-2. Foreign ministers of Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, South Ossetia and Transnistria set up a coordinating body in 2000 and agreed on a commonwealth in 2001. Presidents of three of them founded the Community on 14 June 2006 at Sukhumi. On 27 September 2009 the three agreed to abolish visas for each other's citizens. That is a treaty with a real effect, inside a limited area, because the signatories control their own borders. It gave no one any new way into the wider world. Transnistria's residents, for example, still travel abroad on Moldovan, Russian or other passports. Nagorno-Karabakh, also called Artsakh, ended after Azerbaijan's offensive in September 2023, and its authorities went into exile in Yerevan. Its fellow members did not change that result. Abkhazia and South Ossetia's few recognitions came from states such as Russia and Nicaragua.

A more recent pair is Somaliland and Taiwan, which signed a cooperation agreement in 2020 and exchanged offices. Whether they recognise each other is unclear. Taiwan is a far stronger partner than most, and the deal gave Somaliland practical cooperation. Somaliland then won recognition from Israel on 26 December 2025, a UN member, and that came from that government's own decision. It is not known to have resulted from the Taiwan link.

The Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, founded on 11 February 1991 at the Peace Palace in The Hague, is the other model. Members sign a covenant, including a commitment to non-violence, and receive training and advocacy. It does not claim to make them states. Several original members, including Estonia, Latvia, Armenia and Georgia, later became UN members. Those changes came with the collapse of the Soviet Union. The organisation's own work is voice and training.

Micronations have their own circuit. They sign treaties and non-aggression pacts, send envoys and meet at gatherings such as MicroCon, first held in Anaheim in 2015 and hosted by the Republic of Molossia. Some of their organisations list as many as 80 members. No government treats these as treaties. They are social and creative acts, and harmless if no one sells them as anything more. The risk appears when they are used to back passports or bank licences, as the Dominion of Melchizedek's claims were.

Follow this through for a new community. It signs mutual recognition with ten other unrecognised bodies. Its residents gain a nice document. When a resident's bank asks for a tax residence, an airline asks for a passport or a radio regulator asks for a state's filing, none of these treaties will be accepted, because those systems rely on lists kept by the UN and ISO, or on real states. Reading the text of those systems, it seems that peer recognition would not help anywhere that a recognised state is the gatekeeper.

The potential lies in cooperation among real neighbours and in the record it leaves. The strongest version is a practical treaty between two bodies that actually control land and border posts, covering visas, trade, extradition and shared offices, kept honest and published. That can make daily life easier and it can show governments a pattern of responsible conduct, which is an argument for later recognition. Among bodies with no land it is a way to build a shared culture and little else.

odds.why: Anyone can sign such a paper, so doing so is nearly certain among willing partners. The law score is low because no outside government is bound, and only real breakaway governments even have an argument for treaty capacity. Money does not follow, because banks rely on recognised states. Unions last while their members do, as the end of Artsakh showed, and recognition is decided elsewhere.

zones.name: A government in exile for a community that never had a country
zones.essay:
A government in exile is a political group that claims to be the rightful government of a country, cannot exercise power there, and is based in another country. It usually plans to return. The form appeals to people starting new communities, because it shows that a government can run elections, keep records and collect money without holding any land. So the idea is to use the same machinery for a community that has no homeland to return to, and to set up an administration abroad, in a tolerant host country, with a charter, a cabinet and a register of members.

The Central Tibetan Administration is the working model. It has run from Dharamshala in India since 1959. It has a charter adopted in 1991, courts, a parliament and an elected leader called the Sikyong, and Penpa Tsering was sworn in for a second term in May 2026. Tibetans abroad vote and pay yearly contributions recorded in the Green Book. Money comes mainly from donations, these contributions and aid from governments such as India and the United States for welfare work. No country recognises it as Tibet's sovereign government. The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic, in exile since 1919, shows the same form at low intensity, working as an advocacy group. Poland's government in exile sat in Paris, Angers and London from 1939 until 1990, and disbanded after the fall of communism.

The law gives this form no status of its own. No treaty defines a government in exile or says how it gains standing. In practice its standing depends on whether other states accept its claim, and that claim rests on an existing state or people it says it represents. Poland's government could argue it was the continuing government of a recognised state. A new community has no such state, no territory taken from it and no people with a recognised right to self-determination. Reading the idea through the Montevideo tests, it seems that the form would add nothing. The word "exile" describes being kept away from a territory, and there would be none. Whether an entirely new people could over time claim self-determination is unanswered in any treaty that defines it, since self-determination has no agreed list of who counts, and governments are wary of widening it. So that question is open in theory, and in practice no state is known to have accepted such a claim from a group with no historic link to land.

The host is the central fact. Every member and office sits under host law. Suppose a group registers an association in a friendly country and holds elections. That is ordinary freedom of association. If it calls itself a government and issues passports, the document becomes a problem. In US law it is a crime to falsely make any instrument purporting to be a passport for use, and other countries have similar laws. The Tibetan Green Book is sometimes called a passport and does not let anyone cross a border. An exile body gains nothing by suggesting otherwise. Its ability to tax is also voluntary, since it cannot compel a contribution, and calling a contribution a tax would mislead members, who still owe tax where they live.

Host politics decide the rest. India has reasons to allow the Tibetan administration, and it could change course. Belarus's KGB declared the Rada an extremist group in June 2023, which reaches its members with ties there. A new community with no enemy state has less of that danger, and no rival is likely to bother it. It also has less of the sympathy that brings aid. Governments fund Tibetan welfare work among refugees. A group of volunteers who have chosen to be a nation would have no comparable claim, and its bank will treat it as a private association.

Children and inheritance show how little the form changes. In a new community, a child takes nationality from the parents and the place of birth under ordinary law, and the community's register is a membership record. Wills, marriages and property are handled by the host's law. The community may perform its own ceremonies as a church or association can.

There are real advantages. Holding no land means there is nothing to seize, and the Tibetan and Belarusian cases show such a body can last for decades or a century. It costs little. It can also build the skills of government, such as honest elections and record keeping, and a later chance to hold land, in a zone or on a ship, would find an administration already working. The Sahrawi Republic shows the upper limit, since it has diplomatic relations and a place in the African Union, but it rests on a real people and a real territory recognised as non-self-governing.

The strongest version is modest. It is a registered association in a stable host, with a clear charter, democratic elections, voluntary dues, and an honest statement that it is a government only in its own members' eyes. Over time it could run schools, mutual aid, dispute resolution by arbitration and cultural life. It would then be a diaspora without a homeland, organised like a state. Other countries would have no reason to treat it as one.

odds.why: Setting up a charter and elections abroad is easy if a host tolerates it, so building is near even for a serious group. The law score is low because exile standing rests on a real state or people, and a new community has neither. Funds are limited to voluntary dues, since donors and aid have followed refugees and historic claims. Nothing can be seized, so holding is above even, and recognition is even less likely than for the existing exile bodies.

rules.says: Statehood needs a population, a defined territory, a government and capacity for relations with others.
Falsely making or using any instrument purporting to be a passport is a US crime.

zones.name: A shipboard community where everyone signs one contract
zones.essay:
A ship at sea already works a bit like a small town. The next step would be a community where every resident signs one governing contract, a charter, that sets the rules for life on board, the services, the dues and how disputes are decided. It combines an ordinary flag registration with a private constitution and private arbitration. Nobody claims a new state. The community's rules would sit on top of the flag state's law, much as the rules of an apartment block sit on top of a city's.

Start with what is settled. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), every ship on the high seas sails under a flag, and Article 92 says only the flag state has legal power over it there, with narrow exceptions. Article 94 makes the flag state responsible for safety, crew and seaworthiness. A ship with no flag, or with a micronation's flag, can be boarded by any warship on suspicion of having no nationality under Article 110. So a charter operates under the flag and cannot replace it.

The working model is MS The World, built by shipping professionals. It has 165 residences owned by the people on board, is registered at Nassau in the Bahamas, and is managed from Florida by a company that hires the crew, with an elected residents' board that advises on route and finances. That is a one-contract community in substance, since owners bought into shared rules. It has run since 2002 and claims nothing. Bahamian law applies at sea, and each port's law applies in port. It carries 150 to 200 people and a crew of about 280, so it is small and expensive.

A cheaper version failed on money. Villa Vie's Odyssey ended in October 2026 when its company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea sold 111 cabins and never had a ship, and 78 customers asked US prosecutors to investigate about $16 million in deposits. If the ship or the company goes, buyers of a home at sea have only contract claims against a company.

Insurance can stop it before any government acts. MS Satoshi was bought in 2020 for a floating community in the Gulf of Panama, to sit anchored full-time. Its owner told investors that no protection and indemnity insurer would cover a stationary residential ship. Without that insurance there could be no crew, the ship would lose its class rating and then its flag. No navy was involved. It seems from that case that the insurance market is treating a residential ship as something different from a working vessel, although a moving ship with a professional manager has not met that barrier.

The contract's reach is the interesting part. Under the New York Convention, residents can agree to private arbitration for civil disputes, with a land seat that makes the award enforceable. The contract can set dues and rules and can provide for expulsion at the next port. It can choose a governing law for those matters, subject to what the flag state and courts accept. It cannot reach crime, since the flag state's criminal law applies, and home states often apply their own as well. US law covers offences by or against US nationals in any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation. A private security officer who locks a resident in a cabin risks a charge of unlawful detention unless the flag state's law gives a captain's authority for that case. A captain has traditional powers to keep order on a voyage, and those belong to the captain under the flag's law. The charter could not give them to the community's council.

Reading UNCLOS, it seems that nothing stops a flag state from allowing such a charter, and that a flag state could also pass a special law for a residential ship, as Honduras did for zones on land. No flag state is known to have done so. How far a contract may displace flag state rules on employment or consumer rights is a question for that state's own courts, and no court is known to have considered a charter of this kind. Whether a ship staying at sea for decades, with children born on board, would be treated as a ship or as something else is also unsettled. UNCLOS does not define "ship" in terms of movement. A long-term anchored ship in an exclusive economic zone would invite the argument that it is an installation under the coastal state's control under Article 60. The Thai navy raided a small floating home off Phuket in 2019, and how that case ended is not known.

Then come the indirect routes. Founders and crew remain nationals of their own states, with duties to report income. A US citizen on board still files tax returns every year, and banks report the account. Ports decide who may land and can inspect the vessel. Fuel, food and repairs all come from ports, and supplies can be refused to a ship with legal troubles. A radio licence comes from the flag state. A flag state can strike a ship from its register, and Women on Waves shows that a ship's protection depends on staying in its flag state's good graces, since Dutch law and a Dutch permit gave it legal ground.

Birth and death need thought too. A child born on board takes nationality from parents and from whatever the flag state's law gives. Article 1 of the 1961 statelessness treaty addresses birth on a state's territory, and Article 3 of that treaty treats birth on a ship as birth in the flag state's territory for its purposes. A burial, a will or a divorce goes to a real court.

The potential is solid at the size of a village, and a state is out of reach. The strongest version is a professionally managed ship under a reputable flag, owned by its residents through a company or cooperative, moving regularly, fully insured, with an arbitration clause seated in a respected land jurisdiction. That gives people a floating community of their own rules on most daily matters, able to move away from any single coastal state. It remains under a flag state that it does not control.

odds.why: The World has shown that residents can own a ship and set shared rules, so a charter is feasible for a group with money, and cheaper attempts have failed. The law score matches a ship under a flag, because the flag's law stands above any contract. Banks treat members as residents of their home countries. A flag state or insurer can end the arrangement, and no flag state has yet given a charter special status.

rules.says: A ship sails under one flag, and that state has exclusive legal power over it on the high seas, with exceptions.
A warship may board a ship suspected of having no nationality.
Birth on a ship is treated as birth in the territory of the flag state for that treaty's purposes.
Courts recognise written agreements to arbitrate civil disputes.
