zones.name: A passport or ID accepted by only a few states
zones.essay:
A passport is a request from one authority to others to let its holder pass. It works because governments have agreed to honour each other's, and because a country admitting a traveller knows where that person can be sent back to. A community without recognition could try a different combination. It would issue its own document and persuade just a handful of states to accept it, by agreement or by habit. A person would not need 190 countries. A few places to travel, trade and study might give the community real standing. Four real models show what such a scheme can and cannot do.

The first model is the Nansen passport, the proof that it can work. In 1921 the Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians abroad, including some 800,000 refugees. In July 1922 Fridtjof Nansen, the League of Nations' High Commissioner for Refugees, called a conference in Geneva, and governments agreed on a travel document for stateless people. About 450,000 were issued. Governments promised in advance to honour it, and that promise gave it its force. It gave no citizenship and no right to stay. Its modern descendant is Article 28 of the 1954 statelessness treaty, under which member states issue travel documents to stateless people lawfully staying there, and the treaty's schedule tells other members to recognise them. So the settled rule is plain. A travel document with no state behind it works if states agree to honour it.

The second model is the Haudenosaunee passport, issued since at least 1923, when one went to the Cayuga leader Deskaheh for a trip to the League of Nations. Japan admitted a delegation on it in 2005, Israel accepted it in 2018 subject to Canadian assurances of return, and Ireland accepted it in 2022. Britain refused it in 2010 for the lacrosse team, and the European Union lists it as a fantasy passport. The Israeli condition points to what border officials want. They want another state to promise to take the person back. The strength of this case is a real people with a long political history and sympathy abroad. It also shows that acceptance can vary year by year.

The third is Garry Davis's World Passport, issued by the World Service Authority, which has no agreement with anyone. The Authority claims 189 countries have at some time stamped one, and Foreign Policy reported that a small handful accepted it. A stamp may show only that one officer, on one day, let it pass. Davis was repeatedly arrested and expelled. Supporters said the documents helped refugees, and critics said poor people were charged for paper legally recognised almost nowhere.

The fourth is the partly accepted paper of an unrecognised government. Somaliland issues passports, and South Africa is reported to accept them, though few countries do. Foreign Policy reported in 2014 that Somalilanders had to travel to Puntland to obtain a valid passport for wider use. Transnistria's own papers are not accepted abroad, so residents use Moldovan, Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports.

What stands in the way of a new scheme is practical as well as legal. The strip of letters at the bottom of a passport follows a standard set by the International Civil Aviation Organization, whose Doc 9303 takes issuer codes from the ISO 3166 list and from separate lists for bodies such as the UN. A new community has no code. An airline's check system would not recognise it and the airline, which would pay to return a refused passenger, has good reason not to board the holder. A bank will not accept it as identification. In US law, it is a crime to falsely make any instrument purporting to be a passport for use, and using one at a border can bring charges. In 2002 a group travelling on Elgaland-Vargaland papers, from an art project, was detained in Estonia and sent back the next day. The Dominion of Melchizedek sold passports for up to $3,500, and three people posing as its officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. Sealand's owners revoked theirs in 1997 after finding a laundering ring using them.

There are also proposals aimed at future need. Dirk Messner and Robert Oakes, writing in a paper for the German Advisory Council on Global Change and discussing it at the Katowice climate summit, proposed a climate passport modelled on Nansen's, first for people of small island states whose land may become uninhabitable, offering access and rights equal to citizens' in safe countries. No government is reported to have adopted it. Australia's Falepili Union with Tuvalu offers a different answer, with 280 places a year for residency under an ordinary treaty.

What is open is how few states would be enough, and what an agreement would really give. No treaty sets a number. Reading the Nansen and Haudenosaunee history, it seems that acceptance depends on two things, the state's own political reasons and someone answering for the traveller's return. A community with a real host state that promises to take people back might win limited acceptance from a few partners, under an ordinary bilateral agreement on visas. Whether such an agreement would count as recognising the community is unclear, and a careful state would write that it does not. Whether any state would sign for a private community with no history of need is untested.

The potential is small, and it is greater for people with a real need than for those with a preference. The strongest version is a document issued by a recognised state or an international body for a defined group, such as stateless or displaced members, with signed acceptance by several states, a machine-readable code and a promise of return. A private community's strongest honest version is a membership card plainly labelled as such, used with real passports. Holders of any such card still carry a real nationality for every border that matters.

odds.why: Printing is easy, and winning even three states' written acceptance is hard, which is why building is low. Nansen shows the idea can work when governments agree, and that agreement has come for refugees and historic peoples, not new private groups. Banks will not take such paper as identification. A scheme can last a long time at low level, as the Haudenosaunee and World Service Authority documents have.

rules.says: Issuer codes come from ISO 3166 and separate lists. A new community has none.

zones.name: A digital nation plus a promise that statehood survives lost land
zones.essay:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 10,000 people on low islands that may become uninhabitable within decades. Its answer combines two things. One is a digital copy of the country, with all 124 islands and islets mapped and its culture, language and elders' stories recorded, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them. The other is a legal promise from other states that Tuvalu stays a state whatever happens to its land. The second half is the one that matters in law. People who want a landless nation ask whether this could be a model for them. To answer that, it helps to see exactly what has been decided.

The test for a state, in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, lists a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to deal with others. On a strict reading, a state with no land fails. The Pacific Islands Forum, the regional body, declared in 2023 that the presumption of continuity applies in the context of climate-related sea-level rise. Australia's Falepili Union treaty with Tuvalu, signed on 9 November 2023 and in force on 28 August 2024, commits Australia to recognise Tuvalu's future statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise, and offers residency to up to 280 Tuvaluans a year. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries had legally recognised Tuvalu's digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. These are promises by particular states, and they bind those who gave them.

In its climate advisory opinion of 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice said, at paragraph 363, that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight. Two readings exist, and commentators Syla and Kent set them out. On one view the Court only restated an old rule, that states stay states through occupation or collapse. On the other it accepted that statehood can survive without territory or population in the climate setting. The sentence does not mention sea level or climate, and Judge Tomka questioned whether customary law supports a wider reading, while Vice-President Sebutinde and Judge Aurescu wanted the Court to go further. The International Law Commission's study group on sea-level rise, in a final report in 2025, treated continuity as the answer. In mid-2026 the General Assembly, by resolution 80/263, with 141 states voting in favour, said it "affirms the continuity of statehood in the face of sea level rise". General Assembly resolutions do not bind by themselves, and Britain said the resolution reflects the opinion and does not develop it. Jean-Baptiste Dudant, a former assistant at the Commission writing in a personal capacity, saw growing belief among states that continuity is legally required in these exceptional circumstances alone. So this is moving quickly and is not finished. The legal conditions and consequences of continuity are still unsettled, and no state has yet lost all its land, so the question has never been tested.

For a new project the most important words are "once a State is established". Reading those words, and the General Assembly's context, it seems that continuity protects an existing state and creates nothing. A self-declared online nation has no prior statehood to continue. The digital record gives a real people a means of keeping culture, and Tuvalu's rests on UN membership. That difference rules out the common hope that a digital twin can make a country from scratch. No court has accepted such an argument, and the Montevideo territory test remains in place for new claimants. Estonia's data embassy in Luxembourg is the related state practice, in which a recognised country keeps copies of its records in a protected server abroad under agreement. It also depends on an existing state.

There is also a price, in Tuvalu's case. Under Falepili, Tuvalu agreed to engage with Australia before any security partnership with another state, and former Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said the treaty would undermine its sovereignty. Prime Minister Feleti Teo sought reassurance without revising it. A promise of protection came with a limit on freedom of action, which a small state often accepts for security.

A private group could copy the technique of asking states one at a time for a written promise, and a promise is valuable even if it binds only those who gave it. It could also copy the record keeping, which costs little. A diaspora community with an actual homeland at risk, such as a people on a sinking coast within a larger state, might use the record for cultural survival and argue for rights in law, and it would lack a state's voice in the UN. Suppose a group asks a government to sign a paper promising future recognition. That government would need a reason. Tuvalu's reason is sympathy and a shared interest in Pacific stability. A group with no existing people or place offers neither. Reading what those promises say, a promise to a group that does not yet meet the tests would be a political statement at most, unless other states also act on it.

The potential is high for existing threatened states and very low for new ones. The strongest private version is a partnership with such a state, helping to build its records and services, with the state making the claims. That gives the private group a contract and useful work, and the state holds the sovereignty.

odds.why: These figures are for a new private group copying the model, since Tuvalu is already a UN member. A digital record costs little, and the legal half needs states that already care about a people, which a new group does not have. Paragraph 363 and resolution 80/263 speak of an established state, so the law score reflects only a partnership or an argument by analogy. There is little to seize, so holding is above even.

zones.name: A landless state after sea rise, and communities built on its status
zones.essay:
Suppose a small recognised state loses all its land to the sea and keeps its statehood. That has not happened yet. If it does, the world would hold something new, a full state with a UN seat, a treaty record, a ship register and a nationality law, and no ground under any of them. What follows traces that picture through. It also asks whether such a state could serve as a legal home for other things, such as a ship, a floating platform, a community or a registry, and so offer a route that private founders cannot get in any other way. All of this is prediction from the law as it stands, so the status is untested.

The basis is recent. The International Court of Justice said in July 2025 that once a state is established, losing one of its elements would not necessarily end its statehood. The General Assembly affirmed continuity in the face of sea level rise in resolution 80/263 in 2026, with 141 votes in favour. Neither is binding, and Britain treated the resolution as a reflection of the opinion only. The legal conditions and consequences are unsettled. Judge Tomka doubted that existing practice supports statehood with no territory or population. If continuity holds, Tuvalu keeps its government, and Australia has promised by treaty to recognise it.

Settled practice gives pieces of the answer. A state may hold land in another state as an ordinary owner. Kiribati bought the Natoavatu estate in Fiji for $8.6 million in 2014, and it stayed under Fiji's law. A state may keep government buildings abroad as embassies. A state may also run a ship register from anywhere. Liberia's is managed from Virginia in the United States. A state without any coast may still sail ships under its flag, under Article 90 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Under the same treaty a flag needs a genuine link, in the sense that the state effectively exercises control. The Order of Malta shows diplomatic relations surviving the loss of land since 1798, with extraterritorial buildings in Rome. So a landless government could seemingly keep working, as long as a host lets it sit there.

Several questions are open. No rule says where the government would sit or under what agreement, and a commenter on the 2026 resolution asked this directly, along with where the population would live. If its people spread to other countries on those countries' residence rights, it is unsettled whether they still count as its population. It is also unsettled how its maritime zones would continue, which would decide its fishing income. Nobody has answered these, because no state has reached this point. The International Law Commission's study group said in 2025 that its conclusions could become law if states adopt instruments.

The more unusual hybrid is a landless state using a floating platform as new territory. Under existing law an artificial island is not land and generates no territorial sea, as Article 60 of the Law of the Sea treaty says of installations in the exclusive economic zone. Reading that text, a platform in a state's own surviving exclusive zone would be under that state's authority, as a coastal state's installation. So a drowned state could seemingly license one in its own zone, if its maritime zones are preserved. Whether a platform could count as restored territory for statehood is unanswered and has no case behind it. Kiribati has floated proposals of this kind, and they have not been built.

A private community might try to attach itself to such a state. Here it is useful to separate what a state can sell from what it cannot. It could register the ship, give a flag, license a platform, or naturalise settlers. It could also grant a charter of autonomy, as a host would on land. Those are within its power in theory, subject to its own constitution, its people and its treaties with partners such as Australia, which under Falepili expects to be consulted on security matters. Selling its voice or its UN seat to outsiders is a different thing. Reading what the General Assembly and the Pacific states have said, their support rests on the people of those islands and their right to self-determination. A government that turned into a shell for foreign buyers would risk losing the very sympathy that holds up continuity. States could respond by withdrawing recognition or refusing its ships, as the EU did with Vanuatu's visa waiver when it disliked a passport programme.

The indirect routes all apply. Banks would still need a working regulator. A landless state's register would be checked by port states and insurers. Passports stay valid only while others accept them. A community on its flag would be subject to its law, and members' home countries would still hold their duties.

The potential is real for the state, and small and distant for anyone else. The strongest private version is a respectful contract with a threatened state's government, made with the consent of its people, to help run a registry, build a seat of government, or fund a resettlement community in which those citizens live under their own law as far as the host allows. That would be a service to a state and a real cause. A founder hoping to use it as a shortcut to sovereignty would be relying on events that have not happened, in a state whose people have their own future to decide.

odds.why: These figures are for a private group attached to such a state, which no one has tried and which depends on a land loss that has not happened. The law score is middling because the state could lawfully register or license things, while continuity itself is unsettled. Holding is high if a host and major states keep to their promises. The state itself would already be recognised, and a new group gains no recognition of its own.

zones.name: Banking, insurance and SWIFT for a place nobody recognises
zones.essay:
A place can hold elections and print stamps without other countries' agreement. Paying for imports is different. International payments travel between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks, using the messaging network SWIFT, a cooperative under Belgian law. Each bank is answerable for what passes through it, and it relies on a supervisor in the other country to have checked the customers. Insurance works in a similar chain, since a local insurer passes large risks on to bigger firms abroad. So the question is what routes exist for a place with no recognition, and what combination of a bank, a money transfer company, a neighbour's licence and a phone network can stand in. Real cases give clear answers, and they differ a great deal.

Taiwan shows that recognition is not the deciding factor. Only 11 UN members and the Holy See recognise it, yet according to the US government's trade guide, every Taiwanese bank authorised for foreign exchange has correspondent ties with at least one American bank. Letters of credit are the usual method of payment for established trade, and 31 foreign bank branches were operating there in May 2025. It reaches trade bodies as Chinese Taipei, and at the World Trade Organization under a customs territory name. Taiwan got here with a working regulator, a huge trading economy and foreign partners who want its goods. Reading this case, it seems that a bank's compliance office asks whether a real supervisor stands behind a customer, and that diplomatic recognition matters less than that.

Somaliland sits at the other end. It has run its own government since 1991 and has a central bank and its own shilling, which cannot easily be exchanged abroad. In 2014 Foreign Policy reported that it had no internationally recognised banking sector, no insurance industry and no national post service. Parcels went by DHL through Nairobi or Addis Ababa, and the lack of insurance deterred foreign investors. People relied on money transfer companies, chiefly Dahabshiil, with about $400 million a year in remittances, between 25 and 40 percent of GDP, by officials' estimates. That chain has a weak point. In May 2013 Barclays, one of the last major banks serving such companies, decided to close their accounts, after a record US fine on HSBC. Dahabshiil obtained an injunction from a British High Court that delayed the closing. The risk was that a single London bank's compliance decision could threaten a region's lifeline. The same article said parliament had not yet passed a commercial banking law, for reasons including concern over interest. Mobile money has since spread widely across Somali areas. Somalia, the recognised state, now has thirteen licensed banks, including Dahabshiil International Bank, and is working toward correspondent ties. How far Somaliland's firms rely on that licence is not clear.

Transnistria found a third route, which is to use a neighbour's system. Moldova, which claims the territory, licenses the banks that can reach the outside world. In 2019 the National Bank of Moldova said licensed banks in Chisinau were willing to work with economic operators, including those from the Transnistrian region, on condition that they met anti-money-laundering law and were transparent about their transactions. It added that no permission from any other institution, including in the region, is needed. Trade runs similarly. Since March 2006 Ukraine has accepted goods from Transnistria only with papers from Moldovan customs. Its central bank issues a ruble usable only at home. So the place keeps its own money and government, and its links with the world run through the state it refuses to obey. That state can tighten those links when it chooses.

The settled law here is simple. No treaty gives anyone a right to a correspondent bank. SWIFT sets its own conditions, and as a Belgian company it must follow EU law, which in 2012 and 2022 required it to cut sanctioned Iranian and Russian banks. Reports of the Financial Stability Board show correspondent ties falling each year up to 2018, with small, higher-risk places hardest hit. The Financial Action Task Force lists places with weak rules, and a place it has never assessed has no clean record to show.

What is open is whether an unrecognised place could ever get its own bank onto the system directly, with no state's licence. SWIFT says it serves more than 200 countries and territories and sets its own criteria. Reading that, and Taiwan's position, it seems that recognition is not the formal test and a trusted regulator is. No modern micronation or new project is known to have got this far, and none has a supervisor others accept.

For a new community, the honest order of routes is this. Members keep their accounts in their own countries. The community's company banks in a real country under its rules. It uses a licensed money transfer firm, and it expects to be treated as high risk. Crypto can carry value between members and meets the same rules at the point of cash. Insurance has to come from real insurers, and MS Satoshi shows what happens without it, since with no insurer there was no crew and no flag. A place that wants more must build a real supervisor, adopt anti-laundering law, invite outside review, and seek a neighbour's bank to act as its bridge.

The potential is fair for a place with a real economy and small for a project without one. The strongest version is a host's special zone with its own financial regulator, as in the Dubai International Financial Centre, whose standing comes from Dubai and the UAE. A place with a real population and no recognition can also function for decades on remittances and phones, as Somaliland has, at a cost in investment and in exposure to one foreign bank's decision.

odds.why: Real unrecognised places have working money channels, so this can be done, though a new project with no economy starts far behind them. The law score reflects that no right to banking exists and each link is one firm's decision. Taiwan's full access shows the high end, Somaliland's reliance on remittance firms shows the low end, and Transnistria depends on Moldovan licences. A single bank's decision can cut a link quickly.

zones.name: Contracting with a small state to run a sovereign function
zones.essay:
Some of what makes a country useful can be done by contract. A state holds legal powers that only states may exercise, such as registering ships, sponsoring seabed mining or filing for satellite slots. Nothing stops a state from hiring a private company to run the office. A community or company could therefore aim to get a state's powers working for it without being a state, by making a deal with a small government. This combines a recognised state's legal personality with private management. Unlike most ideas in this field, it has a long and successful record.

The classic case is Liberia's ship register. It was the idea of Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, who set up The Liberia Corporation in 1948 as a joint venture with the Liberian government. Under the deal, 25 percent of revenue went to the government, 10 percent to social programmes in Liberia and the rest to his corporation. The first ship was registered on 11 March 1949. Within 18 years Liberia had the world's largest register. Through two civil wars maritime funds reached about 70 percent of the government's revenue, and it has been described as one of the few legal sources of income for Charles Taylor's regime. Today the register is run by a company called LISCR and is reported to be managed from Virginia in the United States. In 2025 Liberia was again the largest by deadweight tonnage, with 424.1 million tonnes, about 17.4 percent of the world's total. The Marshall Islands started its own register in 1988, and its operator, International Registries, had its management buy it out in 1993.

Other functions followed. The Metals Company reached seabed mining through subsidiaries sponsored by Nauru and Tonga, because a company needs a contract with the International Seabed Authority and a sponsoring state. Tongasat filed for satellite slots through Tonga, since only member states of the International Telecommunication Union can apply. Estonia sells company formation to e-residents worldwide. The Comoros sold nationality to stateless people in the Gulf, in a deal that led to a parliamentary inquiry into missing money. The pattern is settled in the sense that it exists and is legal in the host state, where its own law allows it.

The limits are these. The state keeps the power. A private registry runs on a contract, and the state can end it, as Charles Taylor's government showed when it signed a new contract with LISCR after taking power. The legal duties stay with the state. Under Article 94 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea a flag state must really control its ships, and under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty a state is responsible for what its private actors do in space. So a state that hires out its power remains answerable. If a licensee causes trouble, the state is the one other countries complain to, and it has every reason to cancel.

Then there is the meaning of the genuine link. Article 91 of the Law of the Sea treaty says there must be a genuine link between a flag state and its ships, repeating a 1958 rule that required a state to exercise jurisdiction and control effectively. A 1986 convention intended to strengthen this has not entered force as of 2026. So how little link is enough is open in practice, and much of world shipping sits on the answer. Whether a similar test applies to space licences or to company registers is also unsettled. Adrian Taghdiri wrote in a 2013 note that flags of convenience might arise for spacecraft, and he warned of harm from loose rules.

Suppose a community wants to run its own flag register this way. It signs a contract with a small state's government to manage a special register, for its own ships only. Its ships then fly a real flag and escape the problem of statelessness. Ports, insurers and classification societies check the register's reputation, and a poor one means more port inspections. A new government can cancel the deal and the country's parliament can question it. Radio licences follow the flag. Home countries of staff and owners keep their rules. All this is ordinary shipping law, up to the point where the register looks like a private state's. Reading the treaty, nothing seems to prohibit a state from serving one customer only, and a register of that kind might fail the genuine link test in the eyes of others. No such case is known.

A contract might try to reach further, to immigration, courts or criminal law. Próspera and the Dubai financial zone show that a state can hand over commercial law and courts by its own statute, and Honduras shows it can reverse that. Selling nationality has been tried, and the EU court in the Malta case called it commercialisation inside the EU. Each extension raises the political risk at home, and the host's voters may object, as Honduras's did.

The potential is the most proven in this group of ideas. The strongest version is a narrow, profitable, publicly disclosed contract with a stable small state to run one lawful function very well, with revenue going to that state's people. It gets the operator real legal effect anywhere the state's acts are honoured, including a flag, a sponsor or a slot. The operator gets no sovereignty. The state remains the sovereign and can end the deal.

odds.why: Such deals exist and have lasted over 70 years in Liberia's case, though a new operator needs a willing government and a real business. The law score is high because the state's power is real, up to what its own constitution allows. Money flows normally because the operator is an ordinary company. A new government can cancel, and the operator gains no standing as a state.

zones.name: A zone protected by an investment treaty claim
zones.essay:
A special zone's great weakness is that the state which grants it can take it back. One hybrid tries to fix that by adding outside law. The founders get a host country to sign a long-term stability contract, invest through a company from a country that has an investment treaty with the host, and so gain a right to sue the host in international arbitration if it changes course. This combines a host-granted zone with a treaty claim. The hope is that the threat of an enormous bill will keep any future government from touching the zone.

An investment treaty is a promise between two countries to treat each other's investors fairly and to pay if they take property. ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, is a World Bank body that hears such cases. Governments agreed to this system to reassure investors, and supporters and critics argue over whether it should exist, especially when private tribunals can review a country's laws.

The real test case is Próspera, on Roatán in Honduras. Honduras changed its constitution in 2013 to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development, areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. Próspera's owners, through a Delaware company, relied on a legal stability agreement promising fixed rules and on CAFTA-DR, the trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal in April 2022. Próspera then claimed about $10.8 billion at ICSID. On 20 September 2024 the Honduran Supreme Court held the zone laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. Honduras filed its counter-memorial in July 2026, and the case was still pending in October 2026, with the zone still operating.

The settled parts of this are narrow. A state may reverse its own law, and its courts may strike it down. A treaty cannot stop that from happening. What it offers is a claim for money after the event, if the taking breached the treaty. No tribunal can order Honduras to keep its zone in the sense of sending police to hold it open. A tribunal's award can be enforced against the state's assets abroad, as far as other courts allow.

Reading the dispute, at least three questions appear open in the Próspera case itself, and none has been decided. The first is whether a stability promise made under a law later held unconstitutional from the start counts as a valid promise at all. The second is how far a treaty protects an investment that a country's own highest court has declared had no legal basis. The third is the size of any damages for a project that was only partly built, and the claimed figure has already fallen by about 85 percent. There is also a dispute over consent to arbitration, and a September 2026 report by the International Institute for Sustainable Development described an ICSID tribunal rejecting a Honduran attempt to make its consent under CAFTA-DR depend on first using local courts. Nobody should treat those answers as known until the award is out.

The indirect channels work as follows. The treaty protects investors of the other treaty party, so the nationality of the founders and the registration of the company matter directly. That invites the question of how real a company's home is. A claim also needs a real investment, which requires years of building and the cost of lawyers. Publicity works against the zone, since a claim of billions against one of the poorest countries in the region becomes a national political issue. Próspera became a national issue in Honduras, and neighbours in Crawfish Rock feared losing their land.

The Sulu heirs' case gives a warning about the enforcement stage. Heirs of a sultan obtained a $14.92 billion award against Malaysia in Paris in 2022 based on an 1878 deed. They tried to seize Malaysian assets in France, the Netherlands and Luxembourg and failed, and French courts dismantled the award because no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia. A very large paper victory can come to nothing, and a state with resources will fight it for years. That case rested on an old contract, and a modern treaty claim stands on firmer consent, since the state signed the treaty.

Reading the structure, it seems that its value lies mainly in deterrence. If a future government believes the bill would be real, it may negotiate. Once the zone is repealed and the case begins, what remains is a money claim, and residents get nothing from it directly. A resident's home, business licence and contracts depend on what law the country's courts then apply.

The potential is real as a deterrent. The strongest version has a stable host, a treaty with a major economy, a truly built project, local support won before the deal, and modest terms that a future government would find it easier to keep than to fight. That could produce a long-lasting zone. It remains inside the host state, and its best defence is a local population that wants it there. It offers no path to statehood, and Próspera, the strongest test of the idea, has yet to get a ruling.

odds.why: Investment treaties are real and Próspera has used one, so the structure can be built where a host signs. The law score reflects that the treaty gives a money claim and cannot keep a zone alive. Holding is below even because the host's own courts and later governments can end the zone, as in Honduras, and the case is still undecided. Nothing here creates a state.

cases.name: Harry Schultz, W.G. Hill and the perpetual traveller
cases.founder: Harry D. Schultz; Scope International, publishing as W.G. Hill
cases.story:
A perpetual traveller, sometimes shortened to PT, is a person who bases different parts of their life in different countries and avoids staying long enough in any of them to count as a legal resident. The stated aim is to reduce taxes and civic duties such as jury duty and military service, and to gain personal freedom.

The framing idea is flag theory. It is credited to the investment writer Harry D. Schultz, who proposed that everyone should have a second passport and an address in a tax haven, and that assets should be kept outside the home country. It was later expanded to five flags, adding a place where money is earned and a place where it is spent.

The idea was spread by Scope International Limited, a company in Waterlooville, England. It published books in the 1980s and 1990s under the name W.G. Hill, which may have been a pseudonym, and sold them through classified advertisements in The Times. One of them, published around 1989, was said to have been inspired and edited by Schultz, and a later handbook followed in 1993. Companies marketing offshore centres and tax schemes have used the idea as a staple.

It was never a place and it claimed no territory, so no state ever had to shut it down. The later spread of bank reporting and of residence-based tax tests changed what it can deliver. The evidence for who wrote the books is thin, and the Wikipedia article on the subject itself is marked as needing more citations.
cases.mechanism: Each part of a person's legal life is placed under a different real state. Each state's own rules still apply to the part it holds.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Perpetual traveler

cases.challenge: US indictment over tax, 2024; deferred prosecution agreement, October 2025
cases.name: Roger Ver: citizenship purchase, renunciation and the exit tax case
cases.story:
Roger Ver is an early Bitcoin investor who describes himself as a libertarian and anarcho-capitalist. His case shows what happens when one of the most practised versions of flag theory meets the state the person left.

Ver obtained citizenship of Saint Kitts and Nevis, a Caribbean country that sells citizenship through an investment programme, and in 2014 he gave up his United States citizenship. An Ars Technica headline in January 2015 reported that he could not then get back into the United States. He has lived in several countries, including Japan and Antigua, and he obtained citizenship of Antigua and Barbuda in 2020.

In April 2024 he was arrested in Spain on a US indictment alleging tax evasion. The charges were tax charges. He disputed them, moved to dismiss them, and hired lawyers with close ties to Donald Trump, along with Roger Stone as a lobbyist. On 14 October 2025 he entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice and agreed to pay $49.9 million. Under such an agreement the charges are put aside if the terms are met, so the case did not end in a conviction, and the government later dismissed the indictment.

Two things stand out for anyone thinking about this route. Giving up a nationality did not end the tax claims of the country he had left. A second passport also did not stop an arrest in a third country that has its own extradition arrangements with the United States.
cases.mechanism: Renouncing citizenship does not end a former state's claims for tax it says is owed, and it can pursue them through arrest in a third country.

cases.name: Nottebohm case
cases.story:
Friedrich Nottebohm was a German national who settled in Guatemala in 1905 and lived and did business there for decades. In October 1939, just after the Second World War began, he obtained the nationality of Liechtenstein while on a visit to Europe, and he returned to Guatemala in 1940. In 1943 he was removed from Guatemala under war measures.

Liechtenstein took Guatemala to the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, and claimed compensation on his behalf. A country can bring a claim for a person only through the bond of nationality. The Court overruled Guatemala's first objection in November 1953, and on 6 April 1955 it held Liechtenstein's claim inadmissible.

The Court said that on the international plane a grant of nationality is entitled to recognition by other states only if it represents a genuine connection between the state and the person. Nottebohm had no such connection with Liechtenstein at the time of the grant. His ties were with Guatemala and Germany.

The ruling is narrow, and people often stretch it. It concerned whether Liechtenstein could protect him against Guatemala. It did not say he stopped being a Liechtenstein national in Liechtenstein's law. In the Malta case of 2025 the Maltese government argued that a duty of prior genuine link cannot be drawn from Nottebohm, and the European court decided that case on the basis of EU law. For anyone buying a passport to escape a country, the lesson is that the new passport may be weakest against the country where the person actually lives.
cases.mechanism: A state may give nationality as it likes, and other states need accept it for diplomatic protection only if it reflects a genuine connection.

sources.t: ICJ: Nottebohm (Liechtenstein v. Guatemala)
Judgment in Commission v Malta, C-181/23

cases.challenge: Infringement action in the Court of Justice of the EU
cases.name: Commission v Malta
cases.story:
Malta ran a programme under which a foreigner could gain Maltese nationality, and with it citizenship of the European Union, through set payments and investments. The law behind it was the Maltese Citizenship Act as amended in 2020, with regulations on citizenship for exceptional services. EU citizenship matters because it gives the right to live and work in every member state, and each state must accept the others' grants of nationality. So one country's sale affects all the rest.

The European Commission took Malta to the Court of Justice of the European Union. Malta replied that nationality is decided by each member state's national law, that the treaties do not require a prior genuine link, and that no such duty can be drawn from international law or from the Nottebohm case.

On 29 April 2025 the Grand Chamber ruled against Malta. It said that a state manifestly disregards the special relationship of solidarity and good faith with its nationals when it sets up a naturalisation scheme based on a transaction. The Court said a programme of that sort amounts to the commercialisation of the status of national and, by extension, of Union citizenship. It noted that set payments occupied a key place in the scheme. It declared that Malta had failed to meet its obligations under Article 20 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU and Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union, and ordered Malta to pay costs.

The ruling binds EU member states. It does not apply to programmes elsewhere in the world, whose passports depend on separate visa agreements.
cases.mechanism: Inside the EU, nationality granted for set payments breaches EU law because EU citizenship rests on trust among member states.

sources.t: Judgment in Commission v Malta, C-181/23

cases.passports: Real Comoros passports; nearly 48,000 issued to foreigners according to a parliamentary commission
cases.cost: €4,600 per passport after 2011; first phase meant to earn $200 million
cases.name: Comoros passport sales to the Bidoon
cases.founder: Government of Comoros with the UAE and Kuwait
cases.story:
The Bidoon are stateless people living in Gulf countries, including the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait. Around a decade before 2018, the Comoros Islands, an Indian Ocean country, launched a programme with those two states to sell its citizenship to them, in return for cash to help develop the archipelago. The people receiving this nationality were being given papers by a country far from where they lived.

The first phase was meant to earn the Comoros $200 million in return for giving citizenship to 4,000 stateless families. After a short suspension the scheme went on in 2011 under a new agreement, which set the price of a passport at 4,600 euros and a minimum of 5,000 passports.

In 2018 a commission of the Comoros parliament reported that nearly 48,000 foreigners, mostly Bidoon, had received passports. It said thousands of passports had been sold outside official channels through what it called mafia networks, and that up to $100 million in revenue had gone missing, about 17 percent of a year's GDP. It said secret contracts, poor documentation and the number of groups of officials involved made it hard to find out how much was lost.

This is the nearest real case to one state selling nationality in bulk to a whole group. It shows that paper nationality can be arranged by agreement among governments for people with no link to the country. How the holders have fared since is not known.
cases.mechanism: A state can sell its nationality in bulk to a group by agreement, and the buyers then depend on that state's records and honesty.

cases.laws: Supplement to the Wyoming Limited Liability Company Act
cases.name: Wyoming's DAO company law
cases.story:
In 2021 Wyoming became the first US state to explicitly recognise the legal status of decentralised autonomous organisations, groups that make decisions through software on a blockchain. The act, SEA No. 73, let a DAO register as a new type of limited liability company, the common business form that protects owners' personal assets from the firm's debts. It added a supplement to the state's company law, with rules on formation, articles of organisation, operating agreements, smart contracts, management, voting rights, withdrawal of members and dissolution.

The legislature amended it in 2022 through SEA No. 16. A DAO may now be managed by its members or by an algorithm to varying degrees. The Secretary of State may dissolve a DAO within 30 days of formation if a publicly available identifier is not provided in its filing. The law also set out a way to petition a court for dissolution.

Wyoming's law gave CityDAO the form it used to buy 40 acres near Cody. The law is a company statute and gives no government powers. A DAO company stands where any other company stands under state law, with county zoning, state courts and federal law applying as usual. Its value is in giving a blockchain group a name that can sign a deed and in protecting members from being treated as partners. Legislators elsewhere have looked to it, and Utah, New Hampshire and others later considered different forms.
cases.mechanism: A state gives a software-run group a company's legal body, under that state's law and with a public identifier.

sources.t: Wyoming Legislative Service Office memo

cases.laws: Decentralized Autonomous Organization Act of 2022 and Act of 2023
cases.recognition: Issued by a UN member state
cases.name: Marshall Islands DAO Acts
cases.story:
The Marshall Islands is an independent Pacific country in free association with the United States. It has a history of offering legal products to the world, including a ship register started in 1988. In 2022 it passed a Decentralized Autonomous Organization Act giving blockchain-run groups a legal form, and a further Act in 2023 built on it.

This differs from the US state laws in one way that matters for this subject. The law comes from a member of the United Nations, so a DAO registered there is a legal person of a sovereign state. According to a legal commentary published in November 2023, the 2022 law allowed near-complete anonymity for members, requiring only one person to give know-your-customer details to the registry. The 2023 Act allows series DAOs, where sub-DAOs hold separate assets and liabilities, and it allocates legal risk to the DAO instead of the participants. It also shields DAOs from responsibility for the open-source software they create. A company called MIDAO Directory Services acts as the registrar's office.

Whether courts elsewhere will respect this shield when local people bring claims against a nearly anonymous group has not been tested. The law gives a DAO a home and gives it no authority over land, passports or people.
cases.mechanism: A recognised state can lend its company law to a borderless group, and foreign courts decide for themselves how far to respect it.

cases.name: Utah Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Act
cases.story:
Utah's act was signed on 13 March 2023 and took effect on 1 January 2024. Where Wyoming fitted DAOs into its company law, Utah made a distinct legal entity, the limited liability decentralised autonomous organisation, or LLD. Its authors adapted a model law written by a group called the Coalition of Automated Legal Applications.

An LLD exists as a set of rules encoded on a permissionless blockchain in one or more smart contracts. It may have different classes of members and must be formed by at least one natural person, called a disclosed incorporator. Unlike ordinary small companies, which need not submit their bylaws, an LLD must show the Utah Division of Corporations evidence that its code has undergone quality assurance, and it must provide a public interface for monitoring all its transactions.

Members are liable only for their on-chain contributions, and they are not liable for the acts of other members or for debts beyond the LLD's assets. There is one telling exception. Members who vote for the LLD to refuse a court-ordered remedy may be personally liable in proportion to their governance rights. So the statute that offers the most protection to a software-run group also makes a court's order the point where the protection stops. It gives a community its nearest thing to a constitutional form in US law, and it places that form under the courts of the state.
cases.mechanism: A statute recognises a group defined by its code, and it keeps the courts on top by making defiance of a court order a personal liability.

cases.challenge: US federal court ruling at the pleading stage
cases.name: Samuels v. Lido DAO
cases.story:
Lido DAO runs a service for staking crypto tokens, and its governance token, LDO, is sold on exchanges. A buyer who purchased tokens on the Gemini exchange sued. One argument against the suit was that a DAO is just software, with no legal existence.

On 18 November 2024 the US District Court for the Northern District of California rejected that argument at the motion-to-dismiss stage. It said that Lido's alleged actions were not those of an autonomous software program and were the actions of an entity run by people. The complaint alleged the founders formed the DAO to run a staking service for profit and to distribute revenue, which the court saw as carrying on a business as co-owners. That is the definition of a general partnership, and a general partner can be personally liable for the group's debts.

The plaintiff did not claim every token holder was a partner. The complaint adequately alleged that three large early investors, Paradigm, Andreessen Horowitz and Dragonfly, were partners, because of the part they played in governance. A commentator noted that it is unclear how to separate them from other holders with votes, since a vote alone could arguably make every holder a partner. The ruling is preliminary and the plaintiff's case could still fail. The case shows why groups without a legal wrapper are exposed, and why so many of them seek one.
cases.mechanism: If a group of token holders runs a business for profit, a court may treat it as a partnership, with personal liability, whatever the software says.

sources.t: Eric Goldman: Samuels v. Lido DAO

cases.laws: Juror votes on a blockchain protocol, using the PNK token
cases.name: Kleros and the Mexican court ruling
cases.story:
Kleros is a dispute system built on a blockchain. Jurors are chosen at random from people who hold its token, called Pinakion or PNK, and they review evidence and vote. Its token rewards are meant to encourage honest judgement. Parties can make a smart contract pay out according to the result, so for assets on the chain no court is needed.

The harder question is what a real court does with such a ruling. In a lease signed in Mexico on 1 September 2020, under Mexican law, the parties appointed an arbitrator in the ordinary way and told the arbitrator to use Kleros to decide the substance. When a dispute arose, the arbitrator sent a procedural order to Kleros, which decided in favour of the landlord. The arbitrator used this in a signed award. According to a report by a Mexican attorney published on Kleros's own blog, a local court checked that neither the clause nor the proceedings broke any statute, recognised the award, and ordered enforcement by public force.

A later commentator stressed what this does and does not show. The court enforced the human arbitrator's award and not the blockchain ruling. The same commentator said pseudonymous rulings without a seat may fall outside the New York Convention and may fail its requirement that a party can present its case. The case is one local ruling, reported chiefly by people connected to the project. Kleros has continued to run.
cases.mechanism: A court will enforce a private process when it arrives inside a conventional arbitral award. Pure on-chain rulings remain untested.

sources.t: Kleros: The Kleros case in Mexico
Kluwer Arbitration Blog: Decentralised justice and the New York Convention

cases.laws: Próspera ZEDE Arbitration Statute 2019; Agreement of Coexistence with residents
cases.name: Próspera Arbitration Center
cases.story:
The Próspera zone on Roatán, Honduras, built its justice system on arbitration. Article 20 of Honduras's zone law said zones should use binding arbitration for all matters involving contracts or property. Próspera's charter let its default provider set up original and appeal tribunals for causes of action arising within the zone. Residents sign an Agreement of Coexistence, which appears to be the residency contract the statute refers to, and it includes arbitration by default. The zone and its related bodies also make a standing offer to arbitrate disputes with anyone, which appears to remove the need for a separate agreement in such cases.

The default provider is the Próspera Arbitration Center, a Texas limited liability company. It publishes rules for small claims, evictions, labour and hazardous activity, and it files cases electronically. There are two tracks. The private track is confidential and needs the parties' agreement and a privacy surcharge. The public track looks much like a court, starting with a complaint and summons, and its decisions on zone law are meant to be published and binding as precedents. Practitioners writing about it said they had not found a public database of such awards.

They also noted that Honduras is a party to the New York Convention, and that the public track may raise questions about consent before a foreign court. Arbitration here reaches people who may not have signed a specific clause, which is the opposite of how arbitration normally gets its force. Honduras's Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional in September 2024. How that affects these awards has not been decided by any reported ruling, and the zone continues to operate.
cases.mechanism: A zone can make arbitration its default court system. Its awards then depend on the validity of the zone's law and on foreign courts accepting that the parties consented.

sources.t: Mondaq: Arbitration in Próspera

cases.name: Abolition of the DIFC-LCIA Arbitration Centre
cases.story:
The DIFC-LCIA Arbitration Centre was an arbitration institution in the Dubai International Financial Centre, the separate common-law zone in Dubai. Its name joined the zone with the London Court of International Arbitration, an established English institution.

Decree No. 34 of 2021, effective 20 September 2021, abolished it. Its rights and obligations passed to the Dubai International Arbitration Centre, known as DIAC. Agreements made before that date were deemed valid, and DIAC administers disputes under them unless the parties agree otherwise. Contracts that had named the old centre were suddenly left to work out what they meant.

Courts have since read the decree so as to keep the bargain. In Narciso v Nash (ARB 009/2024), the DIFC Court of First Instance, through Justice Michael Black KC, granted an order on 20 May 2024 stopping a party from pursuing proceedings in Sharjah and gave its reasons on 20 June 2024. It held that a seat in the DIFC implies the DIFC courts as supervisors, that the decree did not void the agreement, and that the parties could use DIAC or another centre.

This is a useful case for anyone relying on private courts inside a state's zone. The arrangement gave real, enforceable justice to many parties, and one decree could still rearrange its institutions. The agreements survived because courts in that same system chose to preserve them.
cases.mechanism: A private court housed in a state's zone depends on that state's decrees, though courts may protect the parties' bargain.

cases.challenge: Jury conviction, Statesville, North Carolina, 18 March 2011
cases.cost: About 16,000 pounds of coins and metals sought in forfeiture, valued near $7 million
cases.name: Liberty Dollar
cases.story:
The Liberty Dollar was a private coin. Bernard von NotHaus minted metal coins and offered them as an alternative to government money. It stands as the main modern example of what can happen when someone offers a private currency to the general public inside a strong state.

On 18 March 2011 a federal jury sitting in Statesville, in the Western District of North Carolina, convicted von NotHaus, then 67. According to the FBI's release, the convictions covered making coins resembling US coins, issuing, selling, possessing and passing Liberty Dollar coins, passing coins intended for use as current money, and conspiracy against the United States. The coins had a current value of about $7 million, and the government sought forfeiture of about 16,000 pounds of coins and precious metals.

The same release said it is a federal violation to create private coin or currency systems to compete with the official coinage. US Attorney Anne Tompkins said that attempts to undermine the legitimate currency of the country are a unique form of domestic terrorism. He was later reported to have been sentenced to probation, according to a coin trade publication. The case was about physical coins that resembled US money, so it does not by itself answer questions about digital tokens with no such resemblance.
cases.mechanism: A state's criminal law reaches private money issued on its soil, especially money that looks like its own.

CoinWeek: Bernard von NotHaus sentenced to probation

cases.stopped_by: US prosecutors with authorities in 17 countries
cases.challenge: Shut down under the Patriot Act, May 2013
cases.name: Liberty Reserve
cases.story:
Liberty Reserve was a private digital currency service in San José, Costa Rica. It billed itself as a payment system for people without bank accounts, and it had over one million users when it was shut. Users could register and move money with only a name, an email address and a birth date, and the site made no effort to verify identities.

Its founder had a prior record in this business. Arthur Budovsky and a partner had run a digital currency exchange called Gold Age from 2002 to 2006 and were indicted in New York in 2006 for operating an illegal financial business. Budovsky moved to Costa Rica and incorporated Liberty Reserve in 2006. Costa Rican authorities told it in 2009 that it needed a licence as a money transmitter, and in 2011 they denied it a business licence over a lack of transparency about its funding. The company formally disbanded at that point in Costa Rica, and Budovsky kept operating.

In May 2013 US federal prosecutors shut it down under the Patriot Act after an investigation across 17 countries. They charged Budovsky and six others with money laundering and with running an unlicensed financial business, and they alleged more than $6 billion in criminal proceeds had passed through.

The case combines a private currency with an offshore base and a host that did not act decisively. The project still lost, because its links to the dollar and to customers ran through places the United States could reach, and because other governments cooperated.
cases.mechanism: An offshore private currency stays within reach when its money flows touch a powerful state's system and when foreign police cooperate.

cases.challenge: US sanctions 2022, overturned on appeal 2024 and lifted 2025; developers prosecuted
cases.name: Tornado Cash and the limits of sanctioning code
cases.founder: Roman Semenov, Alexey Pertsev, Roman Storm
cases.story:
Tornado Cash is software on the Ethereum blockchain that mixes crypto transfers so that it is hard to trace who sent what to whom. In August 2022 the US Treasury placed it on the sanctions list, making it illegal for US citizens, residents and companies to use it. Its domain and code accounts were shut.

On 26 November 2024 the Fifth Circuit appeals court ruled that its immutable smart contracts, programs no one can change, do not count as property under federal law, and that the Office of Foreign Assets Control lacked authority to sanction the software directly, as opposed to the people and groups who abuse it. On 21 March 2025 the Treasury lifted the sanctions and said it remained concerned about North Korean hacking and laundering.

People fared differently from code. Alexey Pertsev was arrested in Amsterdam on 10 August 2022 and sentenced by a Dutch court on 14 May 2024 to 5 years and 4 months. Roman Storm and Roman Semenov were charged in the United States in August 2023 with assisting in laundering about $1 billion. After a three-week trial in 2025, Storm was found guilty of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, one of three charges.

For a project thinking of a crypto treasury, this is the nearest thing to a court test. Software nobody controls proved hard to sanction under one statute in one court. The writers and operators remained open to criminal charges in two countries. How the question would go under other statutes or other countries' laws is not settled.
cases.mechanism: Code that no one controls may fall outside one sanctions statute, and the people who write and run it stay within reach of criminal law.

cases.passports: Issued by the ICRC; Switzerland does not recognise them
cases.recognition: Standing invitation as a UN observer; named in the Geneva Conventions
cases.name: International Committee of the Red Cross and its Swiss agreement
cases.founder: Geneva Society for Public Welfare, 1863; Swiss government agreement, 1993
cases.story:
The International Committee of the Red Cross began in Geneva in 1863, after Henry Dunant's book on the wounded of war. In 1864 sixteen countries met and adopted the first Geneva Convention. Today it is the only institution explicitly named in international humanitarian law as a controlling authority, with a mandate from the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and its own statutes.

It is a private Swiss association, and its governing committee limits membership to Swiss nationals, chosen by the committee itself. Contrary to a common belief, it is not a sovereign body like the Order of Malta. Yet it holds many of the protections of a state. A formal agreement with the Swiss government of 19 March 1993 protects all its property in Switzerland, including its headquarters and archive, grants members and staff legal immunity, exempts it from taxes and fees, guarantees protected and duty-free transfer of goods, services and money, and gives it secure communications at the same level as foreign embassies. Switzerland does not recognise passports it issues.

It holds similar privileges in other countries through agreements or national law, and in some cases through court decisions, such as the right of delegates not to testify before international tribunals. The UN lists it among entities with a standing invitation as an observer.

This is the plainest example of the state-like shield a non-state can earn. The protection was granted for its work, it comes from agreements one government at a time, and it gives no authority over any land or people.
cases.mechanism: A private body gains immunity and treaty standing because states want its service, and it claims no territory in return.

cases.recognition: Non-member observer state at the UN
cases.name: Palestine as a UN non-member observer state
cases.story:
The United Nations lists two non-member states with a standing invitation to take part as observers in the General Assembly and to keep permanent observer missions at its headquarters. They are the Holy See and the State of Palestine. Palestine's status comes from General Assembly resolution 67/19 of 29 November 2012, which accorded it non-member observer state status.

This is a case of a body gaining the word "state" at the UN through a vote of existing members, without full membership, which requires a Security Council recommendation. For the purposes of this subject it shows three things. The status can be voted by a majority of states. A people's claim, its history and wide diplomatic support are what carried that vote. And the status did not settle the disputes on the ground, since control of the territory is a separate question. Governments differ on what the resolution means for statehood, and each decides recognition for itself.

A new project should not read this as a route open to anyone. The status went to a people with a long-standing claim to self-determination and many supportive governments. Taking it as a model would require those same things, and a private founder has none of them. The case belongs here because it marks the upper limit of what a seat near the table can give without membership.
cases.mechanism: A General Assembly majority can give a body an observer seat and the label of state, without membership and without settling its territory.

aka: Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu
cases.recognition: Membership of bodies under agreed names, without recognition as a state
cases.name: The Chinese Taipei formula
cases.founder: International Olympic Committee and Taiwan's Olympic committee
cases.story:
Taiwan's government lost China's seat at the United Nations in 1971, and today only a small number of states recognise it. It still takes part in many international bodies under names worked out for the purpose. The best known is Chinese Taipei.

The Olympic dispute shows how this came about. The International Olympic Committee recognised both the mainland and the Taiwan-based committees in 1954. The People's Republic withdrew in 1958 in protest. At the 1976 Games in Montreal, the host government of Canada refused to let the Republic of China team use that name. In April 1979, at its session in Montevideo, the IOC recognised the People's Republic's committee, and the Nagoya Resolution of that year set out a name for the Taiwan-based committee. Under this arrangement its athletes could keep competing, without their national name, anthem or flag.

The same approach spread elsewhere. Taiwan is a member economy of APEC, the Pacific trade forum, as Chinese Taipei, and it belongs to the World Trade Organization as the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu. Many in Taiwan find the term humiliating and there have been campaigns to change it.

The case shows that a place with no general recognition can sit in functional bodies if their rules allow non-state participants and if the rival state accepts a name. Taiwan's economy and its 23 million people are why others bother. A new small project would have no such weight, although the technique of negotiating a neutral name remains available in principle.
cases.mechanism: International bodies can admit a place under a negotiated name, for a specific function, while leaving its status unresolved.

cases.name: Global Green Growth Institute
cases.founder: President Lee Myung-bak of South Korea
cases.story:
The Global Green Growth Institute began in 2010 as a think tank, started by the then President of South Korea, Lee Myung-bak, to promote what is called green growth, meaning economic growth that protects the environment. In 2012 it was turned into an international treaty-based organisation, in a change formalised at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil.

It now operates under an agreement among its member countries made in 2012. It has an Assembly of all member countries, a Council in charge of strategy, budget and membership, and an Advisory Committee of experts. Membership is open to any UN member state that shares its objectives.

It has nothing to do with founding a territory, and it claims no land and rules no people. It belongs in this subject because it is a clear modern case of a body beginning as a non-state institution and acquiring the legal form of an international organisation by treaty. That conversion needed a sitting head of government and a number of willing states, and it served a purpose those states wanted. Any private founder studying this route should notice those conditions, since a body's standing in this form depends on the states that signed and on nothing it can create for itself.
cases.mechanism: A non-state institute can become an international organisation if states sign a treaty creating it.

cases.cost: 936,000 dunams acquired by the eve of statehood
cases.name: Jewish National Fund land purchases before 1948
cases.story:
The Jewish National Fund is often mentioned when people discuss whether a scattered community could buy its way to a country. It was proposed at the First Zionist Congress in 1897 and formally set up at the Fifth Congress in Basel in 1901, to buy and develop land for Jewish settlement in what was then Ottoman Syria and later Mandatory Palestine. On 8 April 1907 it was incorporated in London as an association limited by guarantee, an ordinary English company form.

It raised money from a worldwide community and bought plots under the law of whoever ruled. In 1939, 10 percent of the Jewish population of Mandatory Palestine lived on its land. By 1948 it owned 54 percent of the land held by Jews there, a bit under 4 percent of the total land of the Mandate. By the eve of statehood it had acquired 936,000 dunams, about 936 square kilometres.

Those figures show why it is a poor model of land producing a state. The State of Israel's creation in 1948 turned on the end of British rule, UN debate and war. Afterwards, in 1949 and 1950, the new government sold what it classed as absentee land to the fund, about 1,000 square kilometres each time, and the legitimacy of these transfers has been questioned. In 1953 the fund was reorganised as an Israeli company.

The history remains deeply contested, with Israeli, Palestinian and other accounts differing on what these events meant. For this subject the narrow lesson is that a diaspora fund can hold land for decades through an ordinary company, under another government's law, and that ownership did not by itself decide who ruled.
cases.mechanism: A diaspora can pool money and hold scattered land through a company for decades. Purchase gave title, and rule was decided by other events.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Jewish National Fund

cases.recognition: Abkhazia and South Ossetia have recognition from a few UN members; Transnistria from none
cases.name: Community for Democracy and Rights of Nations
cases.founder: Presidents of Abkhazia, South Ossetia and Transnistria
cases.story:
The Community for Democracy and Rights of Nations is an organisation of breakaway states on the former territory of the Soviet Union. People often call it the Commonwealth of Unrecognized States or CIS-2, playing on the Russian-led Commonwealth of Independent States. Abkhazia and Transnistria signed a cooperation agreement soon after the war in Abkhazia. In Tiraspol in November 2000 the foreign ministers of Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, South Ossetia and Transnistria set up a permanent coordinating meeting, and in 2001 they agreed in Stepanakert to create the commonwealth. The Community itself was established on 14 June 2006 in Sukhumi by the presidents of Abkhazia, South Ossetia and Transnistria.

Its most concrete act came on 27 September 2009, when the three agreed to abolish visa rules for their citizens. The agreement ran for five years and was then automatically renewed. The leaders also promised economic integration and spoke of seeking membership in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union.

In September 2023 Azerbaijan launched an offensive against Artsakh, as Nagorno-Karabakh was also known, and took the whole territory. Its authorities went into exile in Armenia. Its fellow members did nothing that changed the result. How active the Community remains is not known.

This is the most serious attempt at a mutual recognition circle among places that hold real land. Their mutual agreements work where the signatories control the borders, such as the visa rule. They carry no weight outside that circle, and Russia is the stronger backer of the three remaining members.
cases.mechanism: Unrecognised governments can recognise each other and open their own borders to each other. Outside governments stay unbound.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Community for Democracy and Rights of Nations

cases.recognition: An advocacy body; it has no state standing
cases.name: Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization
cases.founder: Representatives of national movements including Estonia, Latvia, Tibet and East Turkestan
cases.story:
The Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization was formed on 11 February 1991 at the Peace Palace in The Hague. Its founders came from national movements, among them Linnart Mäll of the Congress of Estonia, Erkin Alptekin of East Turkestan and Lodi Gyari of Tibet, together with the international law adviser Michael van Walt van Praag. Its first members included representatives of Estonia, Latvia, Tibet, the Crimean Tatars, Armenia, Georgia, Tatarstan, East Turkestan and East Timor.

Its members are indigenous peoples, minorities and unrecognised or occupied territories, 44 of them in the group's list. Somaliland is among them. All must sign its covenant and commit to non-violence. It advises on recognition and self-rule, trains members in advocacy and security, and raises their human rights cases with international bodies. Its secretariat is in Brussels and The Hague, supported by a foundation set up in the Netherlands.

Several former members later joined the United Nations as the Soviet Union and other arrangements ended. Those outcomes followed much larger events. The group does not grant any legal status, and membership gives no document that a border guard or a bank must accept.

The organisation is a lesson in what a union of the unrepresented can do without any claim of statehood. It gives peoples a place to learn how diplomacy works and a platform to speak, and as an organisation it rests on ordinary association law in its host countries.
cases.mechanism: Peoples without a seat can share advice and a platform through an ordinary association, which grants no status.

cases.name: Polish government in exile
cases.story:
When Germany occupied Poland in 1939, a Polish government formed abroad. It was based in turn in Paris, Angers and London. It opposed German-occupied Poland during the war and then the Soviet-backed People's Republic of Poland after it.

The government in exile went on for about 51 years, far longer than the war that created it. It disbanded after the fall of communism in Poland around 1990. A government in exile is a political group that claims to be the rightful government of a state, cannot exercise power there and sits in another country, and it usually hopes to return one day. This one did see the system it opposed collapse.

Three features matter for anyone studying this form. It began as the government of an existing, recognised state, which gave its claim a legal basis that a brand new group would lack. It relied throughout on hosts, first France and then Britain. And its value lay in keeping a claim alive until conditions changed, while it held no land and governed no one at home. A community with no earlier state could copy the offices, the elections and the long patience, and it could not copy the original claim.
cases.mechanism: An exile government can survive for decades on the strength of a real state's earlier existence and a host's tolerance.

cases.name: Falepili Union
cases.story:
On 9 November 2023 Tuvalu and Australia signed a treaty called the Falepili Union, and it entered into force on 28 August 2024. Falepili is a Tuvaluan word for good neighbourliness, care and mutual respect. The treaty covers migration, climate change and security.

Australia promised three main things. It would provide permanent residency for up to 280 Tuvaluans a year, a pathway meant to allow movement with dignity. It would help Tuvalu in the event of a major natural disaster, a public health emergency of international concern, or military aggression. And it would recognise Tuvalu's future statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise. Prime Minister Feleti Teo described this as the first time a country had committed legally to recognise Tuvalu's future statehood. He said he would seek the same assurance from more countries.

In return Tuvalu agreed to engage with Australia before any partnership, arrangement or engagement with another state or body on security matters, and the two agreed to resolve disputes between themselves without any court or third party. This caused debate. Former Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said it would undermine sovereignty and vowed to repeal it. Teo said he wanted reassurance on sovereignty and later said it might be secured without revising the treaty.

It is the clearest case of a state buying legal assurance about its future existence by treaty. It binds only Australia and Tuvalu. It also shows the usual trade, since a small state gained protection and migration rights and gave up some freedom of action.
cases.mechanism: A state can win a treaty promise that another state will keep recognising it, in exchange for limits on its own foreign policy.
