cases.name: ICJ paragraph 363 and General Assembly resolution 80/263
cases.founder: International Court of Justice and UN General Assembly
cases.story:
No state has ever lost all its land to the sea, so the law had no direct answer to what would then happen to it. In recent years the answer has developed quickly. The Pacific Islands Forum declared in 2023 that the presumption of continuity of statehood applies in the context of climate-related sea-level rise.

In its climate advisory opinion of 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice said at paragraph 363 that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Thirty-three states and seven organisations had addressed statehood in the case, although the question put to the Court did not mention it. Commentators read the sentence in two ways, as a restatement of the ordinary rule or as acceptance that a state can survive without territory. The Court did not mention sea level in that sentence. Judge Tomka questioned the basis for a wider reading in practice, and Vice-President Sebutinde and Judge Aurescu wanted it firmer.

The International Law Commission's study group treated continuity as the answer in a final report in 2025, saying its conclusions could become law if states adopt instruments. The General Assembly then adopted resolution 80/263 in mid-2026, with 141 votes in favour. Quoting the Court, it said it "affirms the continuity of statehood in the face of sea level rise". Britain said it was intended to reflect the opinion and not to develop it.

The legal conditions and consequences of continuity remain open. A commenter asked where a submerged state's population would live and where its government would sit. None of this creates new states.
cases.mechanism: An existing state is presumed to continue after losing land, on growing support. The rule protects established states only.

cases.challenge: British High Court injunction delaying Barclays' closure of accounts, 2013
cases.name: Dahabshiil and Barclays' account closures
cases.story:
Dahabshiil is the largest money-transfer company in the Horn of Africa, with 400 payout locations in the region and its chief executive's office in London. For Somaliland, which has run itself since 1991 with no recognition for most of that time, companies like this are the financial system. Officials there said in 2014 that remittances from abroad came to about $400 million a year, 25 to 40 percent of the economy.

These companies depend on a few ordinary banks in the West that are willing to hold their accounts. In May 2013 Barclays, one of the last major banks still doing so, decided to close the accounts of such operators. A record $1.9 billion fine that US authorities had imposed on HSBC over dealings with banks in Mexico and Saudi Arabia appears to have made the business look too risky for the profits. Dahabshiil went to court, and a British High Court injunction postponed the closure without cancelling it.

The article reporting this quoted Somaliland's planning minister as saying the president had written letters and appealed repeatedly, without result. An unrecognised government had little diplomatic weight with which to press its case. UN agencies, the World Bank and large aid charities also used Dahabshiil to pay their staff and partners, which shows how widely the channel was relied on.

How the dispute finally ended is not known. The case shows that the deciding point for a place with no recognition may be a compliance officer's review in London, far from any ministry.
cases.mechanism: A place with no recognised banks depends on money-transfer firms, and those firms depend on a few Western banks whose compliance decisions can cut off the region.

cases.recognition: A recognised state's flag, run under a private contract
cases.name: The Liberian ship register
cases.founder: Edward Stettinius with the Government of Liberia
cases.story:
The Liberian ship register shows that one of a state's oldest powers can be run as a business from another country. Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, came up with the idea and set up The Liberia Corporation in 1948 as a joint venture with the Liberian government. Of its revenue, 25 percent went to the government, 10 percent funded social programmes in Liberia and the rest went to his corporation. On 11 March 1949 the Greek shipowner Stavros Niarchos registered the first ship under the flag, World Peace.

After Stettinius died in 1949, ownership passed to the International Bank of Washington. Within 18 years Liberia had overtaken Britain as the world's largest register. The civil wars of 1989 and 1999 hurt it, and it fell behind Panama for a period. Maritime funds still supplied about 70 percent of government revenue at one point. After taking over the government, Charles Taylor signed a new registry contract with LISCR, the Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry, and the register has been described as one of the few legal sources of income for his regime.

It is reported to be managed from Virginia. UNCTAD figures for 2025 put it first by deadweight tonnage, at 424.1 million, and an industry table gives it 17.4 percent of world tonnage. The law requires a genuine link between a flag state and its ships, a rule first written in 1958 and repeated in 1982. A 1986 convention meant to strengthen the rule has not entered into force.

The case shows both what renting a state's power can do and who stays in charge, since each new Liberian government holds the contract.
cases.mechanism: A state's legal power can be run by a private firm under contract, anywhere, while the state keeps the power and can change the contract.
